# PART I — INVESTMENT COMMITTEE DECISION

## 1. One-Line Decision

**Decision: Watchlist — a fair-value stock (8.8% cushion) capped by two unresolved Critical governance red flags (an unresolved board-wide fraud allegation and a serial-acquirer pattern), with the scenario math itself showing more downside than upside.**

## 3. Would I Buy This With Real Money Today?

**Final answer: I would not buy this today** because two Critical, unresolved governance red flags sit on top of a stock that is only modestly cheap (8.8% cushion to base fair value) against a much larger downside (30.7% to the near-term bear case, 36.4% to a longer-dated structural floor) — the probability-weighted math nets to roughly breakeven (+1.6% expected return) before any credit is given for the unresolved risks. This is a name to track, not to own.

- **Confidence score:** Understanding 72.5/100 (the business and its numbers are well understood — six modules ran on a mostly-complete, mostly-primary data pool); Conviction 53/100 (capped by the governance flags and the neutral, non-committal nature of a Watchlist call).
- **Position stance:** No position. Do not average in on weakness or chase strength until the two Critical flags resolve or the price moves meaningfully toward the bear case, creating real margin of safety.
- **What would raise confidence:** (1) The derivative lawsuit is dismissed or settled without an adverse finding against the board; (2) the Delivery Hero bridge terms come in at or below the ~4.67% weighted-average coupon on Uber's existing stack, with no new maintenance covenant; (3) the 2026 proxy is filed and shows incentive metrics tied to per-share value (ROIC/FCF-per-share/TSR), not size; (4) a third straight quarter of genuine (ex-UK) cost-of-revenue leverage without a legal-accrual reversal.
- **What would lower confidence further:** (1) The lawsuit survives a motion to dismiss and discovery corroborates the false-disclosure allegation; (2) the bridge is drawn in full and priced above ~5.7%, or a first-ever maintenance covenant appears; (3) a third failed/reversed acquisition after Drizly and Careem; (4) an adverse US driver-classification ruling.
- **What would force exit/rejection (if a position existed):** A proven adverse finding in the derivative litigation, or the illustrative covenant cushion actually breaching once the Delivery Hero financing is finalized — either would force a downgrade to Avoid.

## 4. The Actual Variant Perception

- **What everyone already knows:** Uber is the largest, most profitable ride-hailing/delivery platform, growing Gross Bookings above 20% for four straight quarters, and is buying Delivery Hero in the biggest deal in its history.
- **What is probably priced in:** A slowing, not accelerating, growth story — the market prices just a 5.05% ten-year free-cash-flow growth rate (reverse-DCF, `valuation/05`) and a 10.78% steady-state margin Uber has already beaten on a trailing basis (12.13% TTM EBIT margin). Consensus revenue estimates have also been cut 1.04% in the three trading days after the Q2 print.
- **What the engine thinks may be missed:** Two things pulling in opposite directions, which is exactly why this is not a high-conviction call either way — (1) the reported revenue deceleration (18%→12.2%) is substantially a one-time UK accounting reclassification, not weaker demand, and the market may be under-crediting genuine ~20-25% underlying growth; (2) at the same time, the "clean 4-quarter EBITDA beat streak" the market is implicitly trusting rests on a guided metric that likely still carries a recurring "one-off" legal-reserve add-back (17.3% of Adjusted EBITDA in FY2024, 6.5% in FY2025) that the company stopped even reconciling to GAAP starting Q1 FY2026 — a real quality gap the beat-streak narrative does not price.
- **What evidence would prove the engine is actually different:** If Q3 FY2026 (Nov-03-2026) shows both (a) a genuine, ex-UK cost-of-revenue improvement without a legal-accrual reversal, confirming point (1), and (b) the FY2026 10-K restores the full Adjusted-EBITDA-to-GAAP reconciliation, confirming the quality gap in point (2) either narrows or is disclosed transparently — that would be real, falsifiable evidence the engine's read (accelerating-but-lower-quality) was correct rather than restated consensus.

**Edge score: 35/100.** This is a real, quantified divergence (the UK-optics read and the legal-reserve quality gap are both cited to primary filings), but it falls short of the 50-point proof bar: the "genuine demand" half of the story is priced in loosely, not systematically mispriced, and the "quality gap" half caps upside rather than creating a clean long thesis. **Falsifiable proof:** the Q3 FY2026 print and the FY2026 10-K, as described above — checkable within roughly six months.

## 5. Thesis → Antithesis → Final Thesis

- **Thesis:** Uber's underlying marketplace is compounding — Gross Bookings up 24% for four straight quarters, cost-of-revenue leverage improving, and the market pricing in a conservative 5% ten-year growth rate. Buy the platform business at a fair price.
- **Antithesis:** Two Critical, unresolved governance red flags (a lawsuit naming the entire sitting board, and a $14.8bn debt-funded acquisition that would roughly double gross debt) sit directly on top of that story, and the reported EBITDA beat streak the bull case leans on has a real, unconfirmed quality problem.
- **Revised thesis:** The operating business is real and improving, but this is not a stock to own with real money until the governance overhang clears — the valuation offers only a thin cushion (8.8%) against a much larger downside (30.7-36.4%), so the market is not paying investors to carry the two Critical unknowns.
- **Final thesis:** Watchlist. Track the two binary-ish resolution events (derivative-lawsuit docket, Delivery Hero bridge terms) and the next print; revisit sizing only after at least one of the two Critical flags clears.
- **Insight threshold reached:** the remaining uncertainty is mostly data-dependent, not reasoning-dependent — specifically, the derivative lawsuit's outcome and the Delivery Hero bridge's actual pricing/covenant terms, neither of which primary evidence in this pool can currently resolve.

## 6. Simple Summary

- Uber runs an app that matches riders, eaters, and shippers with independent drivers and couriers, and takes a cut of every trip — it owns no cars or trucks, so it needs very little of its own capital (capex is 0.6% of revenue).
- It may go up because the real demand driver (trips and total bookings) is genuinely speeding up — 24% growth for four quarters running — while the market is pricing in a much slower future than Uber has already delivered.
- It may go down because a federal lawsuit says the CEO, the Chairman, and every director made false statements about ignoring internal safety warnings, and because Uber just agreed to spend $14.8 billion — mostly borrowed — buying Delivery Hero, following one earlier deal (Drizly) that was a total write-off.
- The numbers back up the "real business is fine" half of the story (strong cash generation, low debt today) but not the "everything here is clean" half (the profit number Uber keeps beating includes a "one-time" cost that has shown up two years running, and the company just stopped explaining that number in detail).
- What's missing: the actual terms of the Delivery Hero loan (undisclosed), the 2026 proxy statement (so executive pay can't be checked), and any court ruling on the lawsuit.
- Do not buy now. Wait for the lawsuit's first ruling or the bridge-loan terms, whichever comes first — and note the math itself (a thin 8.8% cushion against a 30-36% downside) does not reward getting in early.
- The single most useful next thing to obtain: the Delivery Hero bridge credit agreement's actual maturity, pricing, and covenant terms (Exhibit 10.2 to the Q2 FY26 10-Q) — it decides whether the balance sheet stays "Adequate" or slides toward real stress.

## 6. Valuation and Peer Mispricing

*(Defers in full to `valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md`.)*

**Verdict: Fairly valued.** Base-case fair value $74.77/share vs. a $68.18 price (2026-08-06, pool-verified) — an 8.82% margin of safety, just inside the ±10% "fairly valued" band. Bull/base/bear (12-month) levels are $104.17 / $74.77 / $47.24, plus a separately-labelled 24-36 month structural-reset (autonomous-vehicle disruption) floor of $43.38. The dominant method is peer-relative NTM EV/EBITDA (38% weight, `03`), cross-checked within 1.2% by an independent own-history-based EV/Sales-implied multiple.

| Metric | UBER | Peer Median (Lyft, DoorDash, DiDi, Grab) | Premium / Discount | Interpretation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| NTM EV/EBITDA | ~10.4x (implied) | ~12.6x | −17.5% | Largely explained by slower forward growth (12.6% NTM vs. DoorDash 22.8%, Grab 25.2%), not inferior quality — Uber has the best credit rating (BBB+) and top LTM EBITDA margin in the set |
| EV/Sales (LTM/NTM) | Premium 38.5% (LTM) / 52.0% (fwd) | — | Premium | Uber converts far more revenue into EBITDA than 3 of 4 peers, so this premium is largely a mirror of the EV/EBITDA discount, not a separate mispricing signal |
| 5-yr own-history EV/Sales | 2.71x current vs. 3.44-3.55x mean/median | — | −21-24% de-rating | Has real, cited fundamental causes (decelerating growth, releveraging), so a full reversion to the historical median should not be assumed |

Three explanations for the modest gap to base fair value: (1) **true, thin mispricing** — the peer-relative method's own convergence with an independent own-history check is a genuine cross-check, not model-fitting; (2) **cycle fear priced correctly** — the forward EV/EBITDA discount is "largely explained by growth, not quality" per the valuation module's own read, so this is not free money; (3) **a real, if modest, governance/M&A discount** — the pending, debt-funded Delivery Hero deal and the unresolved derivative lawsuit are not reflected in any fair-value level above, meaning the "true" risk-adjusted fair value is arguably lower than $74.77 once those are priced, not higher.

**A caution flagged by the valuation module itself:** the sum-of-the-parts (SOTP) reads $48.22/share, 35.5% below the base case — 74.2% of that gap is a single comp-choice artifact (Lyft vs. DiDi for the Mobility comp), but a real, filed $52.3bn capitalized corporate-overhead deduction also drags it down. The SOTP is discounted as a standalone fair-value signal but its underlying finding — Delivery is worth more per forward dollar than Mobility on peer multiples — is kept as informative context.

## 13. Thesis → Antithesis Iteration

### Thesis 1
Uber's operating business is compounding: Gross Bookings up 24% for four straight quarters, cost leverage improving, valuation modestly cheap. Buy.

### Antithesis 1
Two Critical governance red flags (an unresolved board-wide fraud allegation, a $14.8bn debt-funded serial-M&A deal) and a reported-vs-underlying revenue gap that cannot be fully reconciled argue against conviction.

### Revised Thesis 2
The operating story survives scrutiny reasonably well (cash conversion is genuinely strong, the UK revenue optics are disclosed and quantified), but the governance overhang is real, unresolved, and rule-capped — this argues for tracking, not owning.

### Antithesis 2
Even setting the governance flags aside, the scenario math itself (probability-weighted expected return +1.6%, downside risk 36.4%, risk/reward 0.05) does not compensate for the risk being taken — the valuation module's own base case offers only an 8.8% cushion against a 30.7-36.4% downside.

### Final Thesis
Watchlist. The business is real and the near-term operating setup leans constructive, but neither the governance overhang nor the raw scenario math supports initiating a position today. Revisit at the Q3 FY2026 print or on resolution of either Critical red flag.

**Insight threshold reached: the remaining uncertainty is mostly data-dependent, not reasoning-dependent.**

## 14. Math Validation

Executed via Python (see snippet below); the §2 Headline Scorecard, this section, and `decision_record.json` all carry these identical, computed figures — nothing here was re-typed independently.

```
Sum of scenario probabilities:       20% + 40% + 30% + 10% = 100.00%
Probability-weighted target price:   0.20×$104.17 + 0.40×$74.77 + 0.30×$47.24 + 0.10×$43.38 = $69.25
Expected return (from weighted target): ($69.25 − $68.18) / $68.18 = +1.57%
Expected return (sum of p×return):   0.20×52.79% + 0.40×9.67% + 0.30×(−30.71%) + 0.10×(−36.37%) = +1.57%  [reconciles]
Downside risk (−min scenario return): −(−36.37%) = 36.37%
Risk/reward (vs. near-term bear, $47.24): ($69.25 − $68.18) / ($68.18 − $47.24) = 0.05
Margin of safety (base case):        ($74.77 − $68.18) / $74.77 = 8.82%
```

- **Sensitivity to a single assumption:** the entire bull/base/bear_cyclical spread is driven almost entirely by the peer-relative NTM EV/EBITDA multiple applied to consensus NTM revenue (38% weight in the base case) — if that one multiple is wrong by even 1-2x, the base case moves by roughly $6-12/share. The valuation module's own cross-check (an independent own-history-based multiple landing within 1.2%) is the strongest mitigant against this single-assumption risk, but it does not eliminate it.
- **Conclusion: the expected return (+1.6%) is not worth the downside risk (36.4%) at a 0.05 risk/reward** — this is the quantitative reinforcement, independent of the governance caps, for a Watchlist rating rather than any conviction position.

# PART III — MODULE CHAPTERS

## Chapter A: Business Model

**Verdict: Average business — worth deeper work only if valuation is cheap.** No hard disqualifier (0 of 8 tested, 0 of 5 near-misses). Business clarity 75/100, Business quality 46/100 (mixed/average band, capped by competitive-intensity 28/100 and regulatory-dependence 28/100), Moat 60/100 (Narrow, widening), External dependency risk 54/100 (inverted), Capital allocation & governance 50/100 (capped by Filter 4), Data quality 85/100, Overall usefulness 62/100.

Uber runs a two-sided marketplace matching riders/eaters/shippers with independent drivers/couriers/carriers, monetized via a ~27% blended take rate on $193.5bn of FY2025 Gross Bookings. Mobility supplies 57% of FY2025 revenue and 69% of segment profit, with a rising contribution margin on Gross Bookings (7.83%→8.10%, FY24→FY25). Capex is ~0.6% of revenue — the strongest single quality factor — and Uber is the only one of its three named peers (Lyft, DiDi, Bolt) with a positive EBIT margin (12.1% LTM). The moat's own economic test is weaker: 5-year through-cycle average ROIC (CIQ) is just +0.85% against a ~9.7% estimated cost of capital — Uber has cleared its cost of capital only in the last 1-2 years.

**§24 filters tripped:** Filter 4 (serial acquirers) — the pending $14.8bn Delivery Hero takeover, financed by a €14.2bn bridge (~1.2x existing debt), caps Capital allocation & governance at 50/100. Filter 5 (fast-changing industry) — industry rate-of-change scored 32/100 (RF-BQ-005), flagging a sector/technology-cycle bet against unresolved autonomous-vehicle disruption risk (Waymo already runs an independent commercialized fleet).

**Forensic tags fired:** RF-BQ-005 (fast-changing industry). RF-RFS-001 (aggressive accounting practice pattern) — a "non-recurring" legal/regulatory reserve line excluded from Adjusted EBITDA at 17.3% (FY24) / 6.5% (FY25) of that metric two years running, alongside the Q1 FY2026 discontinuation of the full GAAP reconciliation and a +162% (3-year) self-insurance reserve build that management's own MD&A names as the primary driver of a fifth to a third of recent operating-cash-flow "working capital" gains.

**Biggest single risk:** driver/courier reclassification as employees in the US (50.9% of FY2025 revenue) — Uber's own filing states this "would require us to fundamentally change our business model."

Governance Score 43/100, Confidence-Adjusted Score 26/100, Governance Rating **Weak**. Management quality 60/100 (capped from a raw 71), Capital allocation 50/100 (capped from a raw 61), Incentive alignment 5/100 (Insufficient Data — proxy absent), Shareholder friendliness 60/100 (capped), Disclosure candor 53/100, Governance risk 70/100 (inverted), Data quality 65/100, Overall usefulness 68/100.

Management has delivered on the specific promises it makes — four straight years of EBIT/FCF improvement, a 4-for-4 Adjusted EBITDA guidance-beat streak — but M&A has been mixed to value-destructive (Drizly $1.1bn full write-off within 2.5 years; Careem sold to a minority stake in 2023, bought back to control by mid/late-2026) and now culminates in the $14.8bn debt-funded Delivery Hero bid, the largest and least-proven capital-allocation decision in the company's history. Incentives cannot be assessed at all — the 2026 proxy is genuinely absent from the pool. Insiders own 0.18% of the company with zero identifiable open-market cash purchases in six months. The board looks structurally clean (90% independent, split chair, no promoter, no pledging) but is now the subject of an unresolved federal derivative lawsuit alleging the board's own recent proxy statements about safety oversight were false — unproven (confidence 2/5, web-sourced only), but naming the exact people this report is judging.

**This governance verdict is the primary, binding cap on this run's headline rating** — Rating Cap Rules: an unresolved Critical governance red flag caps the headline at Watchlist or lower.

*(Full detail: `analyses/UBER_2026-08-09/management-governance/99_management-governance-synthesis.md`.)*

## Chapter F: Valuation

**Verdict: Fairly valued.** Base-case fair value $74.77/share vs. $68.18 price (8.82% margin of safety). Bull/base/bear (12mo) $104.17/$74.77/$47.24, plus a $43.38 24-36mo structural-reset floor. Valuation attractiveness 54/100, Margin of safety 38/100, Valuation confidence 66/100, Downside risk 58/100 (inverted), Data quality 87/100, Overall usefulness 83/100.

The dominant method is peer-relative NTM EV/EBITDA (38% weight), chosen because it isolates a warranted multiple net of Uber's own revenue-multiple premium and GAAP EPS's mark-to-market noise; it converges within 1.2% of an independently-derived own-history-based check. The current price implies just a 5.05% ten-year FCF growth rate and a 10.78% steady-state margin Uber's trailing 12 months (12.13%) has already beaten — a conservative, achievable bar. The margin of safety (8.82%) is thin against the downside (30.7% to the 12-month bear, 36.4% to the structural-reset floor) — an asymmetry the module states explicitly but does not itself weight or size (that is this synthesis's job, done in §8/§14). The 81.2% raw cross-method spread (SOTP $48.22 to own-history $87.37) is reconciled with two named drivers (a comp-selection artifact and a real $52.3bn corporate-overhead deduction), not silently averaged.

*(Full detail: `analyses/UBER_2026-08-09/valuation/99_valuation-synthesis.md`.)*

## business-model — module synthesis

_Source: `business-model/99_business-model-synthesis.md`_

# Business Model Reality Check — UBER (Synthesis)

## Abstract

Uber runs a two-sided marketplace that matches riders, eaters, and shippers with independent drivers, couriers, and carriers, taking a fee on each transaction without owning vehicles. Mobility supplies 57% of FY2025 revenue and 69% of segment profit, and its contribution margin on Gross Bookings improved to 8.10% from 7.83%. The strongest positive is capital efficiency: capex is roughly 0.6% of revenue, and Uber is the only one of its three named peers (Lyft, DiDi, Bolt) with a positive EBIT margin (12.1% LTM). The strongest negative is durability: five-year average return on capital sits at just 0.85% against a roughly 9.7% cost of capital, and a pending $14.8 billion debt-funded Delivery Hero deal caps the governance score. No disqualifier triggered; this is an average business worth deeper work only if valuation is cheap, given a narrow, still-unproven moat and open driver-classification and autonomous-vehicle risk.

## 1. First-Pass Verdict

### Automatic Disqualifier Check

(Restated from `01_disqualifier-scan.md`.)

| # | Disqualifier | Triggered (Y/N) | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Auditor qualification or going-concern note (last 3 years) | N | PwC unqualified opinion, no going-concern paragraph, FY23–FY25 [FY25 10-K, Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm] |
| 2 | >50% promoter / insider shares pledged | N | No promoter/controlling block; Uber's own policy prohibits insider pledging; the only pledge found is 48% of Aurora stock pledged as note collateral (a corporate financing pledge, not insider equity) [FY25 10-K] |
| 3 | Related-party transactions >25% of revenue or expenses | N | Largest related-party balance (Moove loan, $384M) is 0.7% of FY2025 revenue [FY25 10-K, Notes 6/15/16] |
| 4 | Auditor changed twice in last 3 years without disclosed reason | N | PwC auditor since 2014, unchanged [FY25 10-K] |
| 5 | Material restatement (>5% of revenue or net income) in last 2 years | N | No restatement disclosed; CIQ tag shows "NC" (no change) FY22–FY24 [FY25 10-K; Financials_Annual, Cash Flow tab] |
| 6 | Active regulatory enforcement action on financial reporting | N | Disclosed regulatory matters are privacy/data-related (FTC, DOJ), not financial-reporting enforcement [FY25 10-K, Item 1A] |
| 7 | >40% of revenue from single customer with no long-term contract | N | "No customers accounted for 10% or more of revenue" FY23–FY25 [FY25 10-K, Note 2] |
| 8 | Negative operating cash flow in 3 of last 4 years (excl. growth-stage) | N | Positive OCF all four years: $642M / $3,585M / $7,137M / $10,099M (FY22–FY25) [Financials_Annual, Cash Flow tab] |

No row triggered. The Verdict below is **not** locked by a hard disqualifier.

### Verdict

- **Verdict:** Average business — worth deeper work only if valuation is cheap
- Disqualifier triggered: N
- Business clarity /100: **75** — the take-rate-on-Gross-Bookings model, three-segment structure, and platform KPIs (Gross Bookings, Trips, MAPCs, take rate, segment profit) are clearly disclosed [`02_business-identity.md`; `03_segment-map.md`], offset by a disclosure-quality factor of 67/100 [`07_business-quality.md`] and a mid-stream segment-profit-metric change (Segment Adjusted EBITDA → Segment Operating Income, Q1 FY26) that breaks period comparability [`03_segment-map.md`, §3].
- Business quality /100: **46** *(from `07_business-quality.md`, mixed/average band, capped near 48 by the regulatory-dependence row)*
- Moat /100: **60** *(from `09_moat.md`, strongest individually-scored moat sources — distribution and scale — both at 60; overall verdict is Narrow moat, not Strong)*
- External dependency risk /100 *(higher = worse)*: **54** *(from `10_external-dependency.md`, "material external exposure, mixed mitigation" band)*
- Capital allocation & governance /100: **50** *(from `11_capital-allocation-governance.md`, capped — see rejector-filter cap below)*
- Data quality /100: **85** *(from `00_data-triage.md`, "Sufficient" verdict: FY25 10-K filed Feb-2026, two FY26 10-Qs and two transcripts all within 6 months, no critical missing item)*
- Overall usefulness /100: **62**
- Business type (one line): *(from `02_business-identity.md`)* Two-sided, multi-vertical on-demand marketplace platform (ride-hailing, delivery, freight brokerage) monetized through a take rate on gross transaction value, with an emerging autonomous-vehicle commercialization layer.
- Biggest business-model risk (one line): Driver/courier reclassification as employees in a major market would force Uber to "fundamentally change" its business model [`06_value-chain.md`, §5; `10_external-dependency.md`], compounding with an unresolved AV-driven industry transition scored 32/100 for rate-of-change (Filter 5) where the winner between platform aggregators and vertically integrated AV operators like Waymo is not yet knowable [`07_business-quality.md`, §4].

**REJECTOR-FILTER CAPS (CLAUDE.md §24).**

- **Filter 1 — Crooks / integrity.** Not triggered as a lock. `01_disqualifier-scan.md` routed two soft, unverified adverse signals to management-governance rather than locking: the discontinuation of the consolidated Adjusted-EBITDA-to-GAAP reconciliation starting Q1 FY2026, and an unadjudicated shareholder derivative lawsuit (filed Jul-23-2026) alleging the board ignored an internal ML safety-incident risk model. These cap conviction, not the verdict.
- **Filter 4 — Serial acquirers.** Triggered. `11_capital-allocation-governance.md` scored the acquisition-pattern row 80/100 severity — a multi-year deal cadence (Careem, Postmates, Drizly [wound down], Transplace, Trendyol GO, pending Getir) culminating in the pending $14.8 billion Delivery Hero SE takeover financed by a €14.2 billion committed debt bridge (~1.2x Uber's existing debt stack). Per MODULE_RULES.md this caps **Capital allocation & governance at 50/100** and **Overall usefulness at 70/100** — both applied above.
- **Filter 5 — Fast-changing industry.** Triggered. `07_business-quality.md` scored the industry rate-of-change / disruption row 32/100 (≤40), emitting `RF-BQ-005 (fast-changing industry: rate-of-change ≤40)`. This caps **Business quality at 65/100** (non-binding here — the actual aggregate of 46 is already below the cap) and flags this thesis as a sector / technology-cycle bet rather than a durable compounder: the eventual balance of power between Uber's platform model and vertically integrated AV operators (Waymo already runs a commercialized robotaxi fleet independent of Uber's app) is not yet knowable [`09_moat.md`, §5].

If multiple caps affect the same score, the most restrictive is used. No single score here is hit by two caps simultaneously.

**FORENSIC TAG PROPAGATION (CLAUDE.md §13; eval check AQ).**

- `RF-BQ-005 (fast-changing industry: rate-of-change ≤40)` — fired by `07_business-quality.md`, propagated here per Filter 5 above.
- `RF-RFS-001 (aggressive accounting practice pattern)` — fired by `12_red-flags-sweep.md`. Underlying evidence: a "Legal, non-income tax, and regulatory reserve changes and settlements" line the filing itself labels "distinct from normal, recurring" items was excluded from Adjusted EBITDA at $1,123M (17.3% of FY2024 Adjusted EBITDA) and $564M (6.5% of FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA) for two consecutive years, alongside the Q1 FY2026 discontinuation of the full Adjusted-EBITDA-to-GAAP reconciliation and a fast-growing self-insurance reserve build (+162% in three years, from $4,754M to $12,463M) that management's own MD&A names as the primary driver of a fifth to a third of recent operating-cash-flow "working capital" gains. `RF-DISQ-001` was checked and NOT emitted (0 of 5 quantitative disqualifiers fell in their near-miss band) [`01_disqualifier-scan.md`, §4].

**Module Disconfirmation (CLAUDE.md §8; fix F37).**

- **Strongest bear point:** Business quality scores only 46/100 aggregate, with competitive intensity (28/100) and regulatory dependence (28/100) both scored on the company's own risk-factor admissions of "well-established and low-cost alternatives... low barriers to entry, low switching costs" [`07_business-quality.md`, §1–2]. The moat's own economic test shows Uber's 5-year through-cycle average return on capital (CIQ figure) is just +0.85% against an estimated ~9.7% cost of capital — Uber has cleared its cost of capital only in the last one to two years [`09_moat.md`, §3].
- **Strongest bull point (steelman):** Mobility (57% of revenue, 69% of segment profit) shows a rising, positive contribution margin on the one disclosed proxy unit — 7.83% to 8.10% of $1 of Gross Bookings, FY24 to FY25 [`04_unit-economics.md`, §2–3] — inside a structurally asset-light model (capex ~0.6% of revenue, the strongest single quality factor at 85/100) [`07_business-quality.md`, §1], and Uber is the only one of its three named, CIQ-covered peers (Lyft, DiDi, Bolt) with a positive EBIT margin (12.1% LTM vs. Lyft -2.2%, DiDi -2.6%) [`09_moat.md`, §3].
- **Single killer risk:** Driver/courier reclassification as employees in a major market (the US being the largest at 50.9% of FY2025 revenue) — Uber's own filing states this "would require us to fundamentally change our business model" and force "significant price increases for Riders," with no disclosed cost figure to size the shock [`06_value-chain.md`, §5; `10_external-dependency.md`, §1].
- **Disconfirming evidence already visible:** The red-flags-sweep found that the margin-improvement story several other specialists lean on (business-quality's margin-stability factor, segment-map's segment-margin reads, capital-allocation-governance's leverage-to-EBITDA ratios) rests on an Adjusted EBITDA figure that has excluded a recurring, double-digit-percentage-of-EBITDA "non-recurring" cost line for two straight years, and whose full GAAP reconciliation Uber stopped publishing starting Q1 FY2026 [`12_red-flags-sweep.md`, §2–4].

**CAPITAL STRUCTURE TRANSACTION CAP.** `11_capital-allocation-governance.md` reports the pending Delivery Hero SE acquisition, financed via a €14.2 billion ($15.3 billion) committed debt bridge — roughly 1.2x Uber's existing $12.4 billion debt stack — which would materially change the capital structure **if drawn**. As of the latest realized balance-sheet data in the pool (Mar-31-2026), total debt has moved only from $12,302M (Dec-2025) to $12,419M (Mar-2026), i.e. no realized >50% YoY debt change yet, and the deal is not expected to close until H2 2027. The cap is therefore **not applied on realized numbers today**, but the pending transaction is flagged as a near-term trigger: if the bridge is drawn to fund the deal, gross debt would roughly double and this cap would bind on the next run. The Capital allocation & governance score of 50/100 is already capped by the Filter 4 serial-acquirer rule above for the same underlying transaction — the two rules point to the same number for the same reason and are not stacked.

## 2. Specialist Roll-Up

| disqualifier-scan | No disqualifier triggered (0 of 8); 0 of 5 near-misses in band | Positive OCF all 4 years ($642M→$10,099M FY22–FY25); soft integrity signals (Adj-EBITDA reconciliation discontinuation, unadjudicated derivative suit) routed to governance, not locked |
| business-identity | Two-sided, multi-vertical on-demand marketplace monetized via take rate (~27% blended FY25) on Gross Bookings ($193.5bn FY25) | A single jurisdiction's regulatory/accounting change (UK VAT reclassification) cut reported Q2 FY26 revenue by $1.1bn even as underlying Gross Bookings grew 24% — revenue is partly an accounting construct |
| segment-map | Mobility dominant: 57.0% of FY25 revenue, 69.1% of segment profit | Freight is immaterial and loss-making (-$33M Adj EBITDA FY25); segment profit metric changed basis starting Q1 FY26 (not directly comparable); unallocated corporate cost = 23.7% of segment-level profit |
| unit-economics | Mobility creates value on the one disclosed proxy ($1 of Gross Bookings): contribution margin 7.83%→8.10% FY24→FY25 | True per-trip / per-driver unit economics (acquisition cost, payback, lifetime value) cannot be computed — not disclosed; also corrected an upstream arithmetic error (FY24 Mobility margin is 25.9%, not 22.4%) |

| competitive-map | Holding-to-gaining share vs. Lyft/DiDi/Bolt in the US; not disclosed globally | Uber is the only one of the three CIQ-covered peers with a positive EBIT margin (12.1% LTM); is simultaneously consolidating a named competitor via the pending $14.8bn Delivery Hero acquisition |
| moat | Narrow moat, widening trajectory | 5-year through-cycle average ROIC (CIQ) is only +0.85% vs. ~9.7% estimated WACC — Uber cleared its cost of capital only in the last 1–2 years (FY24 +6.0%, FY25 +9.4%, LTM +10.6%) |

| capital-allocation-governance | Capital allocation concerns — score capped at 50/100 (Filter 4) | Serial-acquirer pattern culminating in the pending $14.8bn Delivery Hero SE takeover funded by a €14.2bn debt bridge (~1.2x existing debt) — large enough to overwhelm the otherwise-improving buyback/leverage/cash-conversion signals if execution disappoints |

## 3. Reconciliation

- **Mobility FY2024 Adjusted EBITDA margin — 22.4% vs. 25.9%.** `07_business-quality.md` and `09_moat.md` both cite "22.4% (FY24) to 26.6% (FY25)" from FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.114. `03_segment-map.md` and `04_unit-economics.md` independently compute 25.9% from the same underlying dollars ($6,497M / $25,087M). `04_unit-economics.md` flags this explicitly as an arithmetic error upstream, not a different figure — the recomputed math ($6,497M ÷ $25,087M = 25.9%) is verifiable and internally consistent with the FY25 figure (26.6%) showing a plausible ~90bp year-over-year improvement, whereas 22.4%→26.6% would imply an implausible ~420bp jump in one year that no other evidence in the pool supports. **Reconciled view: 25.9% is the correct FY2024 Mobility Adjusted EBITDA margin.** The 22.4% figure carried in `07_business-quality.md` and `09_moat.md` should be read as an upstream transcription error; it does not change either report's underlying verdict (both already describe the trend as "improving" and treat FY2025's level as a recent high, not a stable floor).
- **Return on capital — CIQ vendor figure (9.4%/10.6%) vs. own-calculated figure (14.7%).** `09_moat.md` already surfaced and resolved this: the vendor's exact denominator/tax treatment cannot be fully reconciled from the pool, so per the conservative default (CLAUDE.md §4) the lower, vendor-sourced figure is used as the primary read for the moat verdict, with the own-calculated figure shown for transparency. This synthesis carries forward the same conservative choice — the moat verdict's "at-to-modestly-above cost of capital" read uses the lower CIQ figures.
- No other material disagreements between specialists were found.

## 4. Note To The Final Synthesizer

- **Strongest business-model positive:** Mobility's contribution margin on Gross Bookings is positive and rising (7.83% FY24 → 8.10% FY25), inside a structurally asset-light model — capex is ~0.6% of FY2025 revenue and Uber owns no vehicles or trucks, the strongest single quality factor scored (85/100) [`04_unit-economics.md`; `07_business-quality.md`].
- **Strongest business-model negative:** Business quality's aggregate score (46/100) is capped by two factors the company's own risk factors admit directly — competitive intensity (28/100: "well-established and low-cost alternatives... low barriers to entry, low switching costs") and regulatory dependence (28/100: driver reclassification could force a "fundamental" business-model change) [`07_business-quality.md`]. Severity ≥40 red flags from `12_red-flags-sweep.md` that must not be silently dropped: (1) severity 65 — a "non-recurring" legal/regulatory reserve line excluded from Adjusted EBITDA at 17.3%/6.5% of that metric for two consecutive years; (2) severity 55 — a self-insurance reserve build (+162% in three years) that management's own MD&A names as the primary driver of a fifth to a third of recent operating-cash-flow growth; (3) severity 40 — GAAP net income materially moved by unrealized mark-to-market swings on a ~$9.2 billion strategic equity portfolio (Didi, Grab, Aurora, Lucid) unrelated to the core business, with 48% of the Aurora stake pledged and illiquid until 2028 notes settle.
- **Most important segment:** Mobility — 57.0% of FY2025 revenue, 69.1% of segment profit, and the segment with the clearest evidenced (if partial) unit-economics trend [`03_segment-map.md`; `04_unit-economics.md`].
- **Cleanest unit-economics read:** Mobility's contribution margin on $1 of Gross Bookings (the closest disclosed proxy to a per-trip figure, since Uber does not break out Mobility-only trip counts). It "creates value" on this proxy basis but cannot be proven at the strict unit-economics level (acquisition cost and lifetime value are simply not disclosed) [`04_unit-economics.md`, §3].
- **Where the company sits vs. named peers:** Top of the three CIQ-covered peers on margin and capital efficiency — LTM gross margin 40.8% and EBIT margin 12.1% beat Lyft (35.6% / -2.2%) and DiDi (15.6% / -2.6%); Uber is the only one with a positive, disclosed return on capital [`09_moat.md`, §3–4].
- **Main external dependency:** Government/regulatory policy on driver classification and revenue-recognition rules — already demonstrated with a quantified P&L effect (the UK VAT/business-model change cut $1.1 billion of reported revenue in a single quarter) rather than a purely hypothetical risk [`10_external-dependency.md`, §5].
- **Most important capital allocation or governance signal:** The pending $14.8 billion Delivery Hero SE takeover, financed by a €14.2 billion debt bridge (~1.2x Uber's existing debt stack), triggers the Filter 4 serial-acquirer cap and caps Capital allocation & governance at 50/100 — large enough to overwhelm the otherwise-improving buyback discipline and low leverage if integration disappoints, echoing the earlier Drizly wind-down [`11_capital-allocation-governance.md`, §3].
- **Whether any automatic disqualifier triggered:** No (0 of 8; 0 of 5 near-misses).
- **Rejector filters tripped:** Filter 4 (serial acquirers) — tripped, caps Capital allocation & governance at 50/100 and Overall usefulness at 70/100. Filter 5 (fast-changing industry) — tripped (`RF-BQ-005`), caps Business quality at 65/100 (non-binding; actual score is already 46). Filter 1 (crooks/integrity) — not tripped as a lock; two soft signals routed to management-governance to cap conviction only.
- **Biggest missing data point:** A Mobility-only Trip count (or Driver-incentive spend per active Driver), which would let unit economics be tested at the strict acquisition-cost-versus-lifetime-value level instead of the $1-of-Gross-Bookings proxy currently used [`04_unit-economics.md`, §1, §3].
- **Whether the business deserves deeper work, and what would change the answer:** Worth deeper work only if valuation is cheap relative to the risk profile above. What would upgrade the answer toward "High-quality": a Mobility-only unit-economics disclosure proving payback, and/or a full cycle (through a demand downturn) with return on capital sustained above the ~9.7% estimated cost of capital. What would downgrade it toward "Low-quality — avoid": an adverse US driver-classification ruling, or the Delivery Hero deal drawing the full €14.2 billion bridge while integration underperforms (per the pending capital-structure-transaction risk flagged above).

## 5. Simple Summary

- **What it does:** Runs an app that matches riders, eaters, and shippers with independent drivers, couriers, and trucking carriers — Uber owns none of the vehicles.
- **How it makes money:** Takes a cut (a "take rate") of every ride and delivery booked through the app — about 30% on Mobility, 19% on Delivery, and near-zero (pass-through) on Freight, roughly 27% blended in FY2025.
- **Whether each new unit creates value:** Yes on the one measure Uber discloses — each dollar of Mobility Gross Bookings earned 8.10 cents of segment profit in FY2025, up from 7.83 cents in FY2024 — but the strict test (does the profit from each new rider or driver beat what it cost to win them) cannot be checked because Uber doesn't publish that data.
- **Which segment matters most:** Mobility — more than half of revenue and over two-thirds of segment profit; Delivery is real and growing faster but earns less; Freight is small and currently loses money.
- **Whether it has a moat, and against whom:** A narrow, still-young moat built on network effects, scale, and cost advantage against Lyft, DiDi, and Bolt — but the company's own filings admit riders and drivers can and do switch platforms with no lock-in, and the moat has only cleared its cost of capital for the last one to two years, not through a full economic cycle.
- **What external variables it depends on:** Government and regulatory policy above all (driver-classification rulings, tax/VAT rule changes already cut one quarter's revenue by $1.1 billion in the UK alone), plus roughly half of revenue converting from non-US-dollar currencies and a small but genuinely cyclical Freight segment.
- **Whether capital is allocated well:** Mixed — buybacks and low leverage look disciplined day to day, but a serial-acquisition pattern culminating in a $14.8 billion, debt-funded takeover of Delivery Hero caps the governance score at 50/100.
- **Whether it deserves deeper work:** Only if the price is cheap enough to compensate for a mixed-quality, narrow-moat business carrying open regulatory, competitive, and accounting-quality risk.

## business-model / 02_business-identity.md

_Source: `business-model/02_business-identity.md`_

# Business Identity — UBER

## 1. What The Company Actually Does

Uber runs an app-based marketplace that connects people who need a ride, a meal, a grocery order, or a freight shipment moved with the independent drivers, couriers, merchants, and trucking carriers who supply that service. It does not own the cars, drive the deliveries, or own the trucks — it takes a cut of each transaction for matching supply and demand, processing payment, and running the routing/pricing software. As of December 31, 2025 the network covered more than 15,000 cities in over 70 countries, with roughly 34,000 employees supporting hundreds of millions of drivers, couriers, merchants, shippers, and carriers [FY25 10-K, p.1 / Item 1]. The company operates as three reportable segments — Mobility (ride-hailing), Delivery (restaurant, grocery, and retail delivery), and Freight (connecting shippers with trucking carriers) [FY25 10-K, Note 13 (Segment Information)]. Customers pay Uber to solve a coordination problem: finding a nearby driver, courier, or truck fast, at a predictable price, without negotiating or dispatching one themselves. A single cross-platform membership, Uber One, bundles discounts and perks across rides, delivery, and grocery for a subscription fee and had reached 46 million members by year-end 2025 [FY25 10-K, p.1]. In the fourth quarter of 2025, 202 million monthly active platform consumers ("MAPCs") completed at least one Mobility ride or Delivery order [FY25 10-K, p.49].

## 2. How The Company Makes Money

Uber's core formula is a take rate on the total dollar value that flows through its platform (which it calls "Gross Bookings" — total value of rides and deliveries booked, including any Freight revenue, before paying drivers/couriers/carriers):

- **Mobility / Delivery (marketplace segments):** `Revenue = Gross Bookings × Revenue Margin (take rate)`, where Revenue Margin is the service fee Uber keeps after paying drivers/couriers, defined by the company as revenue as a percentage of Gross Bookings [FY25 10-K, p.1 / Item 7A definitions]. For FY2025: Mobility revenue of $29,670 million on Mobility Gross Bookings of roughly $97,497 million (sum of quarterly Gross Bookings disclosed in the 10-K) implies a take rate of about 30% [FY25 10-K, p.58–59 (Certain Key Metrics) and Note 13]; Delivery revenue of $17,248 million on Delivery Gross Bookings of roughly $90,864 million implies a take rate of about 19% [same source]. Blended across all three segments, FY2025 revenue of $52,017 million on Gross Bookings of $193,454 million works out to an overall take rate of about 27% [FY25 10-K, p.49].
- **Freight (logistics-broker segment):** `Revenue = shipment volume × price per shipment`, recognized on a gross basis because Uber acts as principal — arranging and pricing the shipment for the shipper and then paying the carrier as a cost of revenue. Freight revenue effectively equals Freight Gross Bookings by the company's own metric definition ($5,099 million revenue on $5,093 million Gross Bookings in FY2025) [FY25 10-K, p.59 and Note 13].
- **Secondary streams inside the marketplace segments:** advertising sold to merchants and Drivers/Merchants (reported inside Mobility and Delivery revenue) and Uber One subscription fees, both add to Revenue Margin without adding to Gross Bookings volume [FY25 10-K, p.1 (Segment descriptions); Q2 FY26 transcript, prepared remarks].

What drives the volume side is Trips (13,567 million in FY2025, up 20% year-over-year) and MAPCs (202 million in Q4 FY25, up 18%) [FY25 10-K, p.49]. What drives the price/take-rate side is the service fee schedule Uber sets for drivers and merchants, plus how much of that fee is given back as driver incentives and consumer discounts/promotions, which are netted against revenue or booked as cost of revenue depending on the type [FY25 10-K, Note 1 (Revenue Recognition)]. Margin is then a function of how much of the take rate survives after platform-participant payments, incentives, insurance, and fixed platform/technology costs — Adjusted EBITDA margin on Gross Bookings rose to $8,730 million (about 4.5% of Gross Bookings) in FY2025 from $6,484 million in FY2024 [FY25 10-K, p.49].

## 3. Business Type Classification

Two-sided, multi-vertical on-demand marketplace platform (ride-hailing, delivery, and freight brokerage) monetized through a take rate on gross transaction value, with an emerging autonomous-vehicle commercialization layer.

## 3a. Sector Overlay & Required-KPI Checklist

No row in `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md` matches an on-demand, multi-sided mobility/delivery/freight marketplace platform — it is not SaaS, a bank, an insurer, a REIT, a miner, an E&P, a store-based retailer, a telecom, an AUM-based asset manager, or a pharma pipeline business. **No sector overlay for two-sided on-demand mobility/delivery/freight marketplace platform — generic read.** The generic operating-company grammar (volume, price/mix, utilization, segment mix, working-capital cycle) applies, refined by the platform-specific metrics Uber itself discloses and that this pool covers:

| Platform KPI (analogous to a "required KPI" for this business type) | Present / Absent in pool |
|---|---|
| Gross Bookings (total transaction volume) — segment and consolidated | Present — quarterly and annual series by segment [FY25 10-K, p.58–59] |
| Trips | Present — annual total (13,567 million FY2025) [FY25 10-K, p.49] |
| Monthly Active Platform Consumers (MAPCs) | Present — 202 million Q4 FY25 [FY25 10-K, p.49] |
| Revenue Margin / take rate (revenue as % of Gross Bookings), by segment | Present — derivable from segment revenue and Gross Bookings tables [FY25 10-K, p.58–59, Note 13] |
| Segment Adjusted EBITDA / Adjusted EBITDA margin | Present — by segment and consolidated [FY25 10-K, Note 13] |
| Uber One membership count | Present — 46 million as of Dec 31, 2025 [FY25 10-K, p.1] |
| Driver/courier/carrier supply-side metrics (active earners, incentive spend) | Partially present — incentive spend is disclosed as a cost-of-revenue driver; active-earner counts are not separately disclosed in this pool [FY25 10-K, MD&A cost-of-revenue discussion] |
| Cash-paid trip mix (regulatory/collection risk indicator) | Present — approximately 6% of FY2025 global Gross Bookings [FY25 10-K, p.3456 region / Risk Factors] |

None of these are absent to a degree that caps this agent's read; the one partial gap (active-earner supply metrics) is noted but does not block the identity assessment. Sector-specific red flags for this business type, carried forward for downstream agents: driver/courier employment-classification risk (potential reclassification as employees would raise costs materially) [FY25 10-K, p.48 "Driver Classification Developments"]; take-rate compression from competitive discounting or regulatory caps; and Gross-Bookings-to-revenue accounting changes (e.g., a UK Mobility business-model change moved revenue recognition and reduced reported revenue by $1.1 billion in Q2 FY26 alone even as Gross Bookings kept growing) [FY26 Q2 10-Q, p.17094–18587]. Valuation norm for this business type: EV/EBITDA and EV/Gross-Bookings multiples plus a free-cash-flow-based DCF are the standard cross-checks — not a REIT/bank-style method, since Uber owns no real estate or loan book at scale.

## 4. What Drives Variance

Revenue and Adjusted EBITDA moves are driven first by Gross Bookings growth (a function of Trips and MAPCs) — FY2025 Gross Bookings rose 19% (20% constant-currency), driven by Mobility trip volumes (+19%) and Delivery trip volumes (+22%), while Freight Gross Bookings fell 1% on a weak freight cycle [FY25 10-K, p.49]. Second, the take rate itself moves with driver/courier incentive spend, insurance costs (Mobility), and one-off regulatory/accounting reclassifications — the UK Mobility business-model change cut reported Q2 FY26 revenue by $1.1 billion even though the underlying Gross Bookings kept growing at 24%, so a reported revenue "miss" can be a classification effect rather than a demand effect [FY26 Q2 10-Q, p.17094–17099]. Third, mix between segments matters because take rates differ sharply — Mobility runs at roughly a 30% take rate versus roughly 19% for Delivery and effectively 100% (pass-through) for Freight, so a shift in growth toward Delivery or Freight mechanically pulls the blended take rate down even if total Gross Bookings grow [author's calculation from FY25 10-K, p.58–59 and Note 13]. Finally, currency (Uber reports both as-reported and constant-currency growth) and discrete items such as the $5.0 billion Netherlands deferred-tax-asset valuation-allowance release and unrealized gains/losses on minority equity stakes (Aurora, Lucid, Didi, Waabi, Grab) can swing reported net income well away from the operating trend [FY25 10-K, p.49].

# Segment Map — UBER

## 1. Segment Table

Figures below are FY2025 (year ended Dec-31-2025), the latest audited annual filing. Revenue and profit shares are calculated on the sum of the three segments (Mobility + Delivery + Freight), i.e. before the unallocated Corporate G&A and Platform R&D line, which is how the company itself presents Segment Adjusted EBITDA in its reconciliation [FY25 10-K, p.57 (Segment Results of Operations); FY25 10-K, Note 13 — Segment Information and Geographic Information].

| Segment | What It Does | Revenue Share (FY25) | Profit Share (FY25, segment Adjusted EBITDA basis) | Margin Quality | Capital Intensity | Cyclicality | Main Risk |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Mobility | Connects riders with Drivers for car, auto-rickshaw, motorbike, minibus and taxi rides; also includes financial-partnerships products and advertising revenue booked inside the segment [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.29312] | 57.0% ($29,670M of $52,017M) | 69.1% ($7,899M of $11,438M segment-level total) | High — 26.6% Adjusted EBITDA margin on segment revenue ($7,899M / $29,670M), up from 25.9% in FY24 ($6,497M / $25,087M) [FY25 10-K, p.8421–8577] | Mid — asset-light marketplace, but carries driver-insurance and regulatory cost exposure that scales with trip volume [FY25 10-K, p.8706 — insurance expense up $851M YoY] | Mid — tied to consumer discretionary spend and urban mobility demand; management flagged a UK business-model change moving costs from cost of revenue, which cut the reported take rate ~500bp YoY (~400bp of that is the UK optical effect) [Q2 FY26 transcript, CFO remarks] | Autonomous-vehicle disruption to the driver-supply model; competitive/regulatory pressure (e.g. Brazil 2-wheeler competition from DiDi/Meituan) [Q2 FY26 transcript, CEO remarks] |
| Delivery | Food, grocery, alcohol, convenience and retail delivery ("Grocery & Retail"), Uber Direct white-label delivery-as-a-service, and advertising [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.29312] | 33.2% ($17,248M of $52,017M) | 31.2% ($3,572M of $11,438M segment-level total) | Mid — 20.7% Adjusted EBITDA margin on segment revenue ($3,572M / $17,248M), up from 18.0% in FY24 ($2,471M / $13,750M); margin is improving but has a shorter track record of profitability than Mobility [FY25 10-K, p.8446–8591] | Mid — asset-light marketplace; growth partly inorganic (Trendyol GO, Getir, Careem-Delivery reconsolidation), which adds integration and goodwill risk [Q2 FY26 transcript, CFO remarks; FY25 10-K, p.32099] | Mid — less cyclical than Mobility (food/grocery demand is stickier) but exposed to intense local competition (DiDi Food, Meituan vs. iFood in Brazil) [Q2 FY26 transcript, CEO remarks] | Execution risk from the pending Delivery Hero acquisition (announced, expected to close H2 2027, migration through 2029) roughly doubling addressable markets — integration risk is real, not yet in the numbers [Q2 FY26 transcript, CFO remarks] |
| Freight | Connects Carriers (trucking companies) with Shippers; upfront pricing, booking, transportation management and logistics services [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.29312] | 9.8% ($5,099M of $52,017M) | -0.29% (-$33M of $11,438M segment-level total; i.e. a loss) | Low — Adjusted EBITDA margin of -0.6% (-$33M / $5,099M) in FY25, improved from -1.4% in FY24 (-$74M / $5,141M); still loss-making at the segment level [FY25 10-K, p.8465–8613] | Mid — brokerage/marketplace model but earnings highly sensitive to the freight rate cycle | High — explicitly described by the company as being in a "challenging freight market cycle"; FY25 revenue fell 1% YoY [FY25 10-K, p.8758–8769] | A prolonged freight downcycle keeps the segment loss-making; it is immaterial to group profit either way (see Section 2) |

Revenue shares sum to 100.0% ($29,670M + $17,248M + $5,099M = $52,017M total revenue) [FY25 10-K, p.8484–8502]. Segment Adjusted EBITDA sums to $11,438M before the Corporate G&A and Platform R&D deduction of -$2,708M, reconciling to total Adjusted EBITDA of $8,730M [FY25 10-K, p.8620–8667]. Corporate G&A and Platform R&D is 23.7% of segment-level Adjusted EBITDA ($2,708M / $11,438M) — the "Other" / unallocated bucket for profit purposes is large enough to flag (see Section 3).

## 2. Dominant Segment

Mobility is the dominant segment on both measures: 57.0% of FY25 revenue ($29,670M of $52,017M) and 69.1% of FY25 segment-level Adjusted EBITDA ($7,899M of $11,438M) [FY25 10-K, p.8421–8613]. It is not a single-segment business (Delivery alone contributes 33.2% of revenue and 31.2% of segment profit, both material), but Mobility is the clear profit engine — it earns more than twice Delivery's Adjusted EBITDA dollars ($7,899M vs. $3,572M) despite Delivery growing revenue faster (25% vs. 18% YoY) [FY25 10-K, p.8421–8591]. Freight is immaterial to group profit — it lost $33M at the segment level in FY25 and its Adjusted EBITDA is roughly 0% of the group total either way you cut it [FY25 10-K, p.8601–8613]. Most-recent-quarter data confirm the same ranking under the new segment measure: in H1 FY26 (six months ended Jun-30-2026), Mobility Segment Operating Income was $4,244M (68.4% of the $6,206M segment-level total) versus Delivery's $2,016M (32.5%) and Freight's -$54M (-0.9%) [Q2 FY26 10-Q, p.20687–20785].

## 3. Segment Disclosure Quality

Segments are defined consistently across FY24 and FY25 (Mobility, Delivery, Freight, unchanged since at least FY2019 per the CIQ annual segment history) [Uber Technologies Inc NYSE UBER Financials_Annual.xls, Segments tab], but the profit metric changed: beginning Q1 FY26, Uber switched its segment operating performance measure from Segment Adjusted EBITDA to Segment Operating Income, and recast the comparable prior-year periods to match [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Note 10, p.14216–14221]. This is a genuine measurement-basis change, not just a relabeling — Segment Operating Income includes items (e.g., stock-based compensation, certain depreciation/amortization) that Segment Adjusted EBITDA excluded — so FY25 Adjusted EBITDA figures used in Section 1 above are not directly comparable to the FY26 Segment Operating Income figures cited in Section 2; downstream agents should not blend the two without re-basing. The unallocated "Corporate G&A and Platform R&D" bucket is large relative to segment profit — $2,708M in FY25, equal to 23.7% of the $11,438M segment-level Adjusted EBITDA total, and the company explicitly states its allocation methodology "is periodically evaluated and may change," meaning even the segment-to-corporate split is not fixed methodology [FY25 10-K, p.8621–8637]. Profit is disclosed at the segment level (not just revenue), which is a strength, but sub-segment detail is not: Mobility's financial-partnerships and advertising revenue, and Delivery's Grocery & Retail vs. core restaurant-delivery revenue, are described qualitatively but never quantified separately in the filings reviewed [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.29312; Note 1]. Geographic segment revenue is disclosed by region (US & Canada, LATAM, EMEA, APAC) but not cross-tabulated against product segment, so a Mobility-vs-Delivery split by geography cannot be derived from the filings [Uber Technologies Inc NYSE UBER Financials_Annual.xls, Segments tab, Geographic Segments section]. No standalone investor deck is present in the data pool to cross-check the filing splits against a management-facing summary [00_data-triage.md, §3].

## 4. Citations

## business-model / 04_unit-economics.md

_Source: `business-model/04_unit-economics.md`_

# Unit Economics — UBER

## 1. Natural Unit

The natural economic unit for Mobility (the dominant segment — 57.0% of FY25 revenue, 69.1% of FY25 segment profit [`03_segment-map.md`, Section 2]) is **the trip (ride)**: one rider matched to one Driver on Uber's marketplace.

Uber does not disclose Mobility-specific Trip or Monthly Active Platform Consumer ("MAPC") counts — it only reports Trips and MAPCs on a combined Mobility-plus-Delivery basis ("Trips" is defined as "the number of completed consumer Mobility rides and Delivery orders in a given period" [FY25 10-K, "Certain Key Metrics"]). That means a true Mobility-only Gross Bookings-per-Trip or contribution-margin-per-trip figure **cannot be computed from filings**. What Uber does disclose at the Mobility-segment level, every quarter, in dollars: Gross Bookings (the total dollar value of Mobility rides, before Uber's cut), Revenue (Uber's cut), and Segment Adjusted EBITDA / Segment Operating Income (profit after Driver payments, incentives, insurance and other variable costs). This report therefore builds the required table using **$1 of Mobility Gross Bookings** as the measurable proxy unit — the closest available substitute for "one trip" given the disclosure gap, and itself a legitimate unit (comparable to how an asset manager's unit is "$1 of AUM"). This substitution is stated explicitly, not smoothed over, per the missing-disclosure item named in Section 3.

Delivery's natural unit is the order (one meal, grocery, or retail delivery); Freight's is the load (one truckload booking). Both face the same disclosure limit — Uber does not report Delivery-only or Freight-only Trip/order counts either.

## 2. Unit Economics Table

Unit = $1 of Mobility Gross Bookings, unless noted. Mobility Gross Bookings are built by summing the four disclosed quarters of each fiscal year: FY24 = $18,670M + $20,554M + $21,002M + $22,798M = $83,024M; FY25 = $21,182M + $23,762M + $25,111M + $27,442M = $97,497M [FY25 10-K, "Certain Key Metrics," Gross Bookings by segment table]. This reconciles exactly to the $193,454M FY25 total Gross Bookings figure once Delivery ($90,864M) and Freight ($5,093M) are added, confirming the segment split is internally consistent.

| Unit Economic | Value | Period | Direction vs Prior Year | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue per unit (Mobility revenue as % of Mobility Gross Bookings — Uber's own "Revenue Margin" definition, i.e. the take rate) | FY25: 30.4% ($29,670M / $97,497M); FY24: 30.2% ($25,087M / $83,024M) | FY24 vs FY25 | Improving (+21bps) at the full-year level. Separately: Q2 FY26 25.4% ($7,363M / $28,988M) vs Q2 FY25 30.7% ($7,288M / $23,762M) — down ~530bps | FY25 10-K, MD&A "Segment Results of Operations," p.57–58 and "Certain Key Metrics" Gross Bookings table; Q2 FY26 10-Q, MD&A "Mobility Segment" (Q2 FY26 revenue $7,363M per Q2 FY26 10-Q Note 10; prior-year Q2 FY25 revenue derived as $7,363M − $75M disclosed increase = $7,288M) |
| Gross margin per unit | Not disclosed at Mobility-segment level | — | Unknown | FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.112: "The CODM does not evaluate operating segments using asset information" — and Uber does not publish a segment-level cost-of-revenue split either, only the consolidated figure ($26,651M FY24 → $31,338M FY25, 61%→60% of total revenue) [FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.54] |
| Contribution margin per unit (Segment Adjusted EBITDA / Segment Operating Income as % of Mobility Gross Bookings — nets out Driver payments and incentives, insurance, network costs, and credit-card processing, so it is the closest disclosed proxy to a contribution margin, though it also carries some allocated advertising and headcount cost) | FY25: 8.10% ($7,899M / $97,497M); FY24: 7.83% ($6,497M / $83,024M). On the new Segment Operating Income basis (adopted Q1 FY26): Q2 FY26 7.64% ($2,215M / $28,988M) vs Q2 FY25 (recast) 7.28% ($1,729M / $23,762M, derived from the disclosed $486M / 28% increase) | FY24 vs FY25; Q2 FY25 vs Q2 FY26 | Improving in both periods (+27bps FY24→FY25; +36bps Q2FY25→Q2FY26) | FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.113–114; Q2 FY26 10-Q, Note 10 and MD&A "Mobility Segment"; corroborated in Q2 FY26 transcript, CFO Q&A: "our mobility operating income margin remains very strong at 7.6%" (2,215/28,988 = 7.64%, matching within rounding) |
| Cost to acquire / build the unit (Driver incentive spend, rider acquisition cost) | Not disclosed per driver or per rider — only the aggregate year-over-year dollar change is given: Driver payments and incentives (recorded in cost of revenue) increased $1.6 billion in FY25 | FY25 | Unknown (cost is rising in aggregate dollars, but that is explained by rising Gross Bookings, not a disclosed per-unit rate) | FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.54–55: "a $1.6 billion increase in Driver payments and incentives that are recorded in cost of revenue... as a result of increased Mobility Gross Bookings" |
| Payback period or unit lifetime | Not disclosed — no rider/Driver cohort, retention, or lifetime-value data is published | — | Unknown | Not proven from available data |

## 3. Value Creation Read

**Creates value**, on the one basis Uber actually discloses — but the read is partial. Every disclosed year since Mobility Adjusted EBITDA was first broken out, the segment has earned a positive and slowly rising profit on every dollar of Gross Bookings it books: 7.83% in FY24 rising to 8.10% in FY25, and 7.28% rising to 7.64% on the newer Segment Operating Income basis between Q2 FY25 and Q2 FY26 [FY25 10-K, Note 13; Q2 FY26 10-Q, Note 10]. Because Driver payments, incentives, insurance and network costs — the largest variable costs tied to each ride — are already netted out of that margin, a positive and improving figure is meaningful evidence that incremental Gross Bookings are profitable at the margin, not just at scale. What the math cannot prove is the classic contribution-margin-times-lifetime-versus-acquisition-cost test required to call this "value creation" in the strict unit-economics sense: Uber discloses neither a Driver- or rider-acquisition cost nor a rider/Driver retention curve, so there is no way to check whether the profit earned per dollar of Gross Bookings recovers what was spent to win that dollar in the first place. The single most valuable missing disclosure is a Mobility-specific Trip count (or Driver-incentive spend per active Driver) split out from the combined Mobility-plus-Delivery Trips figure Uber currently reports — without it, "creates value" here rests on a marketplace-dollar profitability trend, not a proven unit-level payback.

The margin trend itself is short: it has risen for roughly three to four years running since Uber returned to consistent Mobility profitability, not across a full economic or competitive cycle, so the 8.10% figure should be read as a level achieved during a period of strong post-pandemic demand recovery and market-share consolidation, not assumed as a permanent floor.

## 4. Sensitivity

The take rate (Mobility revenue as a percentage of Mobility Gross Bookings) is the input most likely to move the value-creation read if it shifts 20%, and it has already shown it can: a single regulatory change — Uber's UK business-model change effective January 2, 2026 — cut the take rate by roughly 530 basis points in one quarter (Q2 FY25's 30.7% to Q2 FY26's 25.4%), of which management attributes about 400 basis points to an accounting reclassification (moving cost out of cost of revenue, an "optical impact" per the CFO) and the remaining roughly 100 basis points to a deliberate pricing choice — investing in lower-cost offerings such as Moto in Brazil [Q2 FY26 transcript, CFO Q&A]. On the cost side, Driver payments and incentives (+$1.6 billion in FY25) and insurance expense (+$851 million in FY25, driven by "an increase in insurance rate per mile and miles driven") are the two variable-cost lines management calls out as growing fastest [FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.54–55]; insurance cost per mile is a structural risk unique to Mobility (Uber flags that "inflation has increased and is expected to increase our insurance costs" as a general risk factor) and is not something Uber controls the way it can dial Driver incentives up or down. Of the two, the take-rate move is the more historically volatile of the two on the evidence available — it produced a five-hundred-basis-point swing in a single quarter from one jurisdiction's regulatory change, a bigger one-period move than either disclosed cost line.

**Reconciliation note (CLAUDE.md §4/§20):** this report's FY24 Mobility Adjusted EBITDA margin recomputed directly from `03_segment-map.md`'s own cited figures ($6,497M / $25,087M) is 25.9%, not the 22.4% stated in that report's Section 1 table. Both reports cite the same source (FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.114); this appears to be an arithmetic error upstream rather than a different figure. This report uses the recomputed 25.9% (and the resulting FY24→FY25 direction of "improving," not the larger jump upstream's figure would imply) — flagged here rather than silently overridden.

# Customer And Geography Map — UBER

## 1. Customer Map

| Customer Type | Importance (% of revenue if disclosed) | Long-term Contract? (Y/N/Not disclosed) | Evidence | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Individual riders and eaters (Mobility + Delivery consumers, ~hundreds of millions of monthly active platform consumers) | Not concentrated — filing states no single customer reaches the 10% disclosure threshold | N — pay-per-transaction, no contracts | "No customers accounted for 10% or more of revenue for the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025." [FY25 10-K, Note 2 (Summary of Significant Accounting Policies), Concentration of Credit Risk] | Low on a single-customer basis — revenue is spread across 202 million monthly active platform consumers in Q4 FY25 [FY25 10-K, p.1] |

[FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors] | Medium — company itself flags this as a risk, but with no cited percentage it cannot be sized |

No customer-type revenue breakdown (e.g., "X% from restaurants," "Y% from grocery") is disclosed in the FY25 10-K. The filing's only quantified customer-concentration statement is the negative one above (no single customer ≥10% of revenue).

## 2. Geography Map

|---|---:|---|---|---|
| United States and Canada ("US&CAN") | 50.9% ($26,469m of $52,017m) | Declining share — down from 54.8% (FY2023) and 53.7% (FY2024), even as dollar revenue grew 12.1% year over year [FY25 10-K, Note 13, Geographic Information] | $20,436m (FY23) → $23,618m (FY24) → $26,469m (FY25) [FY25 10-K, Note 13] | Medium — still the largest single region; "large metropolitan areas" risk factor concentrates exposure within this region and others |
| Europe, Middle East and Africa ("EMEA") | 31.5% ($16,364m of $52,017m) | Growing share — up from 26.6% (FY2023) to 28.5% (FY2024) to 31.5% (FY2025); dollar revenue grew 30.6% year over year, the fastest of the four regions | $9,904m (FY23) → $12,529m (FY24) → $16,364m (FY25) [FY25 10-K, Note 13] | Medium — fastest-growing region also carries the most regulatory/accounting change risk (see UK note below) |
| Asia Pacific ("APAC") | 11.3% ($5,857m of $52,017m) | Growing, roughly stable share — 11.9% (FY2023) → 11.5% (FY2024) → 11.3% (FY2025); dollar revenue grew 16.3% year over year | $4,429m (FY23) → $5,036m (FY24) → $5,857m (FY25) [FY25 10-K, Note 13] | Low-Medium |
| Latin America ("LatAm") | 6.4% ($3,327m of $52,017m) | Growing dollars, stable share — 6.7% (FY2023) → 6.4% (FY2024) → 6.4% (FY2025); dollar revenue grew 19.0% year over year | $2,512m (FY23) → $2,795m (FY24) → $3,327m (FY25) [FY25 10-K, Note 13] | Low-Medium — FX and macro volatility typical of the region |

**Single-country breakdown also disclosed** (a finer cut of the same total revenue, by country rather than region):

| Country | % of Revenue (FY2025) | Trend | Evidence |
|---|---:|---|---|
| United States | 45.7% ($23,771m) | Declining share — 49.9% (FY2023) → 48.7% (FY2024) → 45.7% (FY2025) | [FY25 10-K, Note 13, Geographic Information] |
| United Kingdom | 20.4% ($10,609m) | Growing share and fastest dollar growth — 17.5% (FY2023) → 19.0% (FY2024) → 20.4% (FY2025); +26.7% YoY | [FY25 10-K, Note 13] |
| All other countries (combined) | 33.9% ($17,637m) | Roughly stable share — 32.6% (FY2023) → 32.2% (FY2024) → 33.9% (FY2025) | [FY25 10-K, Note 13] |

Regional and country cuts both reconcile to total FY2025 revenue of $52,017 million [FY25 10-K, Note 13]. No individual country other than the US and UK is broken out — "all other countries" spans over 70 countries in which Uber operates [FY25 10-K, p.1], so no further single-country concentration can be assessed below the UK line.

Additional geography-adjacent concentration disclosed in Item 1A: "In 2025, we generated 15% of our Mobility Gross Bookings from trips that either started or were completed at an airport" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors] — a channel concentration inside the US&CAN/EMEA/APAC mix, not a separate country.

## 3. Concentration Flags

| Concentration Flag | Triggered (Y/N) | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| One customer >20% of revenue | N | "No customers accounted for 10% or more of revenue for the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025." [FY25 10-K, Note 2, Concentration of Credit Risk] |
| Top 3 customers >40% of revenue | Not assessable | Uber does not disclose customer-level revenue shares at all — the business is a consumer marketplace with no top-3-customer concept in the way a B2B supplier would report it |
| One geography >50% of revenue | Y (borderline) | US&CAN = 50.9% of FY2025 revenue [FY25 10-K, Note 13] — just above the 50% line, and its share has been declining each of the last three years (54.8% → 53.7% → 50.9%) |
| One customer or geography >30% with no long-term contract disclosed | Y | US&CAN (50.9%) and EMEA (31.5%) both exceed 30% of FY2025 revenue, and revenue in both is transaction-by-transaction with no long-term customer contracts disclosed — this is structural to the marketplace model, not a company-specific gap [FY25 10-K, Note 13; Note 2] |

## 4. Read

Uber's concentration risk is geographic, not customer-based: no single customer clears even the 10% disclosure threshold because revenue comes from hundreds of millions of individual, pay-per-transaction riders and eaters [FY25 10-K, Note 2]. Geographically, the business still leans on the United States and Canada for just over half of revenue (50.9% in FY2025) and the UK alone for a further 20.4% — together 71.3% of revenue sits in two of the four regions — though the US share has been shrinking each year as EMEA (led by the UK) grows faster [FY25 10-K, Note 13]. This geographic weight is naked in the sense that it rests on transaction volume, not contracts — there is nothing locking in next year's US or UK Gross Bookings — and the company's own risk factors flag both a "large metropolitan areas" dependency and, within Delivery, an unquantified reliance on "a limited number of large restaurant groups and other merchants" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A]. The single biggest dependency the synthesizer should know about is the US + UK combination (66.1% of FY2025 revenue) sitting inside a business model where a single regulatory or accounting change in either market — as already happened with the UK Mobility revenue-recognition change that cut Q2 FY26 reported revenue by $1.1 billion even as Gross Bookings kept growing [FY26 Q2 10-Q, p.17094–17099] — can move consolidated results without any change in underlying demand.
