## business-model / 06_value-chain.md

_Source: `business-model/06_value-chain.md`_

# Value Chain Position — UBER

## 1. Stages Occupied

| Value Chain Stage | Company Role (1 sentence) | Bargaining Power vs Upstream | Bargaining Power vs Downstream | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Platform / marketplace — Mobility | Matches riders with independent drivers, sets the take rate (~30% of Gross Bookings) and the dispatch/pricing algorithm, but owns no vehicles [Business Identity output, §2]. | Mid | Mid | Driver supply constraints force Uber to raise incentives in many markets and it cannot always reduce them without hurting liquidity; regulators have imposed per-mile/per-minute minimum driver-pay rules and Uber itself says forced employee reclassification would require "significant price increases for Riders" to offset the cost [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors — Driver Classification Developments, p.11; Item 1A — driver-pay minimums]. On price, some municipalities cap surge pricing (e.g., Honolulu bans surge in emergencies) [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors — Regulatory]. |
| Platform / marketplace — Delivery | Matches consumers with restaurants/merchants and couriers, takes a roughly 19% take rate on Delivery Gross Bookings [Business Identity output, §2]. | Weak–Mid | Weak–Mid | "A significant amount of our Delivery Gross Bookings come from a limited number of large restaurant groups and other merchants, and this concentration increases the risk of fluctuations in our operating results" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors — Driver/Merchant/Carrier Supply]. On the consumer side, "an increasing number of municipalities have proposed delivery network fee caps with respect to our Delivery offering" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors — Regulatory Obstacles]. |
| Platform / marketplace — Freight brokerage | Acts as principal broker: contracts with Shippers at a set price, then contracts separately with independent Carriers and is on the hook for the Carrier's payment regardless of whether the Shipper pays [FY25 10-K, Note 1 (Revenue Recognition) — Freight]. | Weak | Weak | Freight revenue fell 1% in FY2025 "due to lower revenue per load as a result of the challenging freight market cycle," and Freight Adjusted EBITDA improved only $41 million (a ~55% year-on-year gain off a small base) even as Carrier payments fell $66 million in lockstep with revenue [FY25 10-K, MD&A — Freight Segment, FY2025 vs FY2024]. Segment economics move with the trucking spot-rate cycle, not with anything Uber controls. |
| Emerging AV commercialization layer | Distribution/demand channel and anchor capital provider for third-party autonomous-vehicle (AV) technology and OEM partners (Waymo in Austin/Atlanta, Nuro/Lucid, Zoox, Wayve, Baidu, Pony, Verne, Rivian, and others), rather than a technology developer itself. | Mid, improving | Not yet assessable | Uber is spending roughly $10 billion over a multi-year period, split between equity stakes in AV software partners and balance-sheet support (fleet ops, real estate, ~120,000 vehicle offtake commitments) for OEMs; management states "for every dollar that we have invested, our partners have been able to raise an additional $2.50 from other investors," and explicitly frames the multi-partner strategy as insurance against dependence on any one AV provider — "we want to make sure that we're not dependent on one partner" [Q2 FY26 transcript, prepared remarks and Q&A, CFO Balaji Krishnamurthy and CEO Dara Khosrowshahi]. |

Bargaining power bands:
- **Strong:** Company sets price, dictates terms, has alternatives
- **Mid:** Negotiated outcomes, no extreme leverage either way
- **Weak:** Price-taker, terms imposed, few alternatives

## 2. Input Cost Pass-Through

Uber's largest input cost — payments and incentives to Drivers and Couriers — moves mechanically with Gross Bookings rather than through a negotiated pass-through clause: FY2025 cost of revenue rose $4.7 billion (18%), made up of a $1.6 billion increase in Driver payments/incentives and a $1.6 billion increase in Courier payments/incentives, both simply tracking higher Mobility and Delivery Gross Bookings [FY25 10-K, MD&A — Cost of Revenue, FY2025 vs FY2024]. Insurance — Uber's second-largest controllable-but-volatile input — is not automatically passed through either way: in FY2025 a $851 million increase in insurance expense (driven by a higher insurance rate per mile and more miles driven) pressured Mobility Adjusted EBITDA [FY25 10-K, MD&A — Mobility Segment, FY2025 vs FY2024], while by Q2 FY26 the CFO described insurance as having "become a tailwind this year," with the company choosing to "reinvest the savings from insurance back into the market" — i.e., into lower effective prices and driver/consumer incentives in markets like California, Los Angeles, and San Francisco to drive trip growth, rather than banking the windfall as margin [Q2 FY26 transcript, CFO Balaji Krishnamurthy, prepared remarks]. This is a discretionary reinvestment decision, not a contractual escalator or indexed-pricing clause — no such clause is disclosed in this pool for either Mobility or Delivery. Freight is the one segment with mechanical, near-total pass-through: Carrier payments are booked as cost of revenue and moved down $66 million in FY2025 in step with the $42 million fall in Freight revenue, consistent with Uber's stated role as principal that invoices Shippers a gross fee and separately owes Carriers a freight charge regardless of Shipper payment [FY25 10-K, MD&A — Freight Segment; Note 1 (Revenue Recognition) — Freight].

**Supplier / input concentration (quantify).** The filing does not disclose a percentage of cost of revenue or purchases attributable to any single Driver, Courier, merchant, or Carrier — Not proven from available data; the underlying supply base (individual drivers/couriers, and independent trucking carriers) is inherently fragmented by design, which limits single-supplier concentration risk on that side. The one qualitative concentration flag the 10-K itself raises is on the Delivery merchant side: "a significant amount of our Delivery Gross Bookings come from a limited number of large restaurant groups and other merchants" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors — Driver/Merchant/Carrier Supply], but no percentage of Delivery Gross Bookings or revenue tied to the largest merchant or top-3 merchants is disclosed — a real gap, not an invented number. A second, structurally different dependency is technology infrastructure: Uber "does not control the physical operation of any of the co-located data centers we use or the operations of our third-party service providers," may "not be able to easily switch to another cloud or data center provider," and its co-located data-center agreements are "of limited durations" with "no obligation to renew... on commercially reasonable terms or at all" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors — Third-Party Cloud/Data Center Dependency]. No specific vendor is named and no percentage of infrastructure spend is quantified, but the switching-cost and non-renewal language is itself evidence of a real, if unquantified, dependency — this is the closest thing to a material single-source input risk visible in the pool, and it feeds the bargaining-risk discussion in §5. On the AV side, the ~$10 billion multi-year commitment is spread across at least seven named partners (Waymo, Nuro/Lucid, Zoox, Wayve, Baidu, Pony, Verne, Rivian), which management frames explicitly as diversification against dependence on any one AV supplier [Q2 FY26 transcript, Q&A] — a deliberate hedge against the concentration risk that would otherwise exist in a single-partner AV strategy.

## 3. Customer Pricing Power

Uber's blended take rate was about 27% of Gross Bookings in FY2025 (Mobility ~30%, Delivery ~19%, Freight effectively pass-through) [Business Identity output, §2, from FY25 10-K, p.49, p.58–59, and Note 13], and management's own framing in the most recent call is to defend the "net" take rate rather than push it higher: asked about a nearly 500-basis-point year-on-year decline in reported Mobility revenue margin, the CFO attributed most of it to a UK business-model accounting change (an optical, not economic, effect) and to "deliberate investments... in our lower-cost offerings," and told investors to focus on the net take rate disclosed in the 10-Q, which "will largely show take rate remaining broadly stable" [Q2 FY26 transcript, CFO Balaji Krishnamurthy, Q&A]. That same call disclosed no unilateral headline price increase in the last 24 months; instead, management described actively growing lower-cost products — Wait & Save (trading time for a lower fare) in the US, and two-/three-wheeler and Moto-brand rides in Brazil and other markets — because "low-cost products continue to grow globally," which is evidence of price-sensitive demand at the margin rather than pricing power [Q2 FY26 transcript, CEO Dara Khosrowshahi, Q&A]. The UK Mobility business-model change itself cut reported Q2 FY26 revenue by $1.1 billion even as underlying Gross Bookings kept growing 24%, illustrating that a chunk of "revenue" is a regulatory/accounting classification outcome rather than a price Uber freely sets [FY26 Q2 10-Q, cited in Business Identity output, §4]. Net: Uber can raise or lower its effective take rate at the margin through incentive spend and product mix, but the direction of travel in FY2025–FY2026 has been toward cheaper products and stable-to-flat net take rate, not toward tested, standalone price increases.

## 4. Economic Control Verdict

**Mixed.** In its core Mobility and Delivery marketplaces Uber sets the fee schedule and controls the pricing/dispatch algorithm, giving it real discretion over how a cost swing (e.g., the FY2025 insurance cost spike, or the 2026 insurance tailwind) flows through to margin versus reinvestment [FY25 10-K, MD&A; Q2 FY26 transcript]. But that discretion sits inside hard constraints on both sides: driver-pay minimums and classification litigation cap how far it can squeeze the supply side, delivery-fee and surge-pricing caps proposed or enacted by municipalities cap the demand side, and Delivery is disclosed as dependent on "a limited number of large restaurant groups" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors]. Freight is unambiguously squeezed — a pass-through brokerage earning a thin, cycle-driven spread with a ~2% Adjusted EBITDA margin on segment revenue in FY2025 (own calculation: $41 million improvement off an implied ~$75 million FY2024 base, versus $5,099 million FY2025 segment revenue) [FY25 10-K, MD&A — Freight Segment; Business Identity output, §2].

## 5. The Single Biggest Bargaining Risk

Driver/courier employment reclassification: Uber's own 10-K states that being forced to treat Drivers as employees would require "significant price increases for Riders to offset" the added cost, directly testing whether Uber's take-rate discretion survives contact with a mandated, non-negotiable cost shock across every affected jurisdiction at once [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors — Driver Classification Developments, p.11].

## business-model / 07_business-quality.md

_Source: `business-model/07_business-quality.md`_

# Business Quality — UBER

Upstream inputs read: `02_business-identity.md` (business type classification and sector-overlay check), `03_segment-map.md`, `05_customer-geography.md` — all present. No upstream gap to flag.

**Sector overlay (step 2b):** `02_business-identity.md` already tested Uber against every row in `frameworks/SECTOR_OVERLAYS.md` and found no match — Uber is not SaaS, a bank, an insurer, a REIT, a miner, an E&P, a store-based retailer, a telecom, an AUM-based asset manager, or a pharma pipeline business. **No sector overlay for two-sided on-demand mobility/delivery/freight marketplace platform — generic 11-factor scoring applies**, refined only by the platform KPIs Uber itself discloses (Gross Bookings, Trips, MAPCs, take rate/Revenue Margin, Uber One membership) that this report uses as evidence.

## 1. Quality Factor Table

| Quality Factor | Score /100 | Evidence | Comment |
|---|---:|---|---|
| Pricing power *(higher = better)* | 50 | Uber sets the take rate itself (Revenue Margin ≈30% Mobility, ≈19% Delivery, FY2025) and has raised it — Mobility Adjusted EBITDA margin rose from 22.4% (FY24) to 26.6% (FY25) [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.114; business-identity §2]. But the same filing states the industries it competes in have "well-established and low-cost alternatives... low barriers to entry, low switching costs, and well-capitalized competitors in nearly every major geographic region" [FY25 10-K, p.2478]. | Some demonstrated ability to keep more of each transaction dollar, capped by an explicit filing admission that customers can switch cheaply. |
| Repeat / recurring revenue *(higher = better)* | 55 | 13,567 million Trips in FY2025 against 202 million MAPCs (Q4 FY25) implies very high per-user usage frequency [FY25 10-K, p.49]. Uber One membership reached 46 million by year-end 2025, bundling discounts across rides, delivery, and grocery for a subscription fee [FY25 10-K, p.1]. No long-term contracts exist with individual riders or eaters — every transaction is discrete and cancellable [customer-geography §1, Concentration of Credit Risk note]. | High habitual repeat usage and a genuine subscription layer (Uber One), but the underlying revenue is transaction-by-transaction, not contracted — this is repeat behavior, not contractual recurrence. |
| Customer stickiness *(higher = better)* | 35 | Filing states directly: "the low switching costs between competitor platforms or services" are a risk to Driver and consumer retention [FY25 10-K, p.2666]. Riders and Drivers commonly multi-home across Uber, Lyft, Bolt, Didi, Ola with no lock-in mechanism beyond habit and Uber One perks [FY25 10-K, p.1763, p.2502]. | Weak stickiness by the company's own admission — no contracts, no switching cost, and named low-cost competitors in every major region. |
| Margin stability *(higher = better)* | 50 | Consolidated EBITDA margin (CIQ definition) moved from -70.6% (FY16) through -2.8% (FY22), 5.2% (FY23), 8.0% (FY24), to 12.1% (FY25) and 13.5% (LTM Jun-26) — a long run of losses followed by four consecutive years of steady, real improvement [Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab, CIQ export]. A one-off UK Mobility revenue-recognition change cut reported Q2 FY26 revenue by $1.1 billion even as Gross Bookings grew 24% [Q2 FY26 10-Q, p.17094–17099, cited in business-identity §4]. | Recent-year trend is genuinely stabilizing and improving, but the decade-long history was deeply unstable, and even now a single accounting reclassification can swing reported revenue by over a billion dollars in one quarter — headline margins need reading with that noise in mind. |
| Capital intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 85 | Capital expenditure was $336 million (FY24) and $308 million (LTM) against FY2025 revenue of $52,017 million — roughly 0.6% of revenue [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab, CIQ export; FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.114]. Uber owns no vehicle or trucking fleet — Drivers, couriers, and Carriers own and maintain the assets [segment-map §1]. Segment-level asset data is not disclosed because "the CODM does not evaluate operating segments using asset information" [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.112]. | Structurally asset-light marketplace — the strongest factor in this scorecard, though segment-level capital efficiency can't be verified from filings directly. |
| Competitive intensity *(low intensity = high score)* | 28 | "The mobility, delivery, and logistics industries are highly competitive, with well-established and low-cost alternatives that have been available for decades, low barriers to entry, low switching costs, and well-capitalized competitors in nearly every major geographic region" [FY25 10-K, p.2478]. Named rivals include Bolt, Didi, Lyft, Ola in ride-hailing, plus DoorDash-class competitors in Delivery, and Alphabet (Waymo), Amazon (Zoox), and Tesla developing competing autonomous-vehicle platforms [FY25 10-K, p.1763, p.2502, p.2529]. | The company's own risk factors describe a structurally crowded, low-barrier field — this is not a defensible-adjective call, it is the filing's own characterization. |
| Industry rate-of-change / disruption risk *(low rate-of-change = high score)* | 32 | Uber "may fail to offer autonomous vehicle technologies on our platform at competitive scale, fail to offer such technologies... before our competitors, or such technologies may fail to perform as expected" [FY25 10-K, p.2229, p.2739]. Waymo has already launched its own commercialized robotaxi fleet independent of Uber's platform, alongside a partnership arrangement it also runs through Uber's app [FY25 10-K, p.2744]. If AV technology matures, competitors "could allow competitors to offer such services at a substantially lower price" [FY25 10-K, p.2744]. | Autonomous vehicles are actively reshaping who can win in ride-hailing over the next several years, and the long-run winner (platform aggregator vs. vertically integrated AV operator like Waymo) is not yet knowable — a live technology race, not a settled industry structure. |
| Regulatory dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 28 | Driver-classification litigation is active across the US (California, Massachusetts), France, Netherlands, Switzerland, Mexico, and New Zealand; a November 2025 New Zealand Supreme Court ruling found drivers are employees while logged into the app [FY25 10-K, p.2463, p.2468]. Reclassification "would require us to fundamentally change our business model" [FY25 10-K, p.2458]. Mexico passed a law in December 2024 to reclassify higher-earning mobility/delivery workers as employees with profit-sharing rights [FY25 10-K, p.2463]. | The single largest structural risk to the cost model — an adverse ruling in a major market could force a step-change in driver-related costs, and this is litigated simultaneously in many jurisdictions, not a contained one-off. |
| Commodity dependence *(low dependence = high score)* | 78 | Drivers and couriers own their vehicles and bear fuel costs directly — Uber's own cost of revenue does not carry a direct fuel or vehicle line [segment-map §1, capital-intensity discussion]. Exposure is indirect: high fuel prices raise Driver cost pressure, which Uber may need to offset with incentives, a cost it does disclose as a driver of take-rate compression [business-identity §4]. | Not a commodity-price business in the way a miner or airline is — the commodity exposure sits mostly on the supply side (Drivers) and reaches Uber's P&L only indirectly through incentive spend. |
| Cyclicality *(low cyclicality = high score)* | 47 | FY2020 (COVID) revenue fell to $11,139 million from $13,000 million in FY2019, a 14.3% decline, before recovering to $17,455 million in FY2021 [Financials_Annual.xls, Income Statement tab, CIQ export]. Freight — 9.8% of FY2025 revenue — is explicitly cyclical: management attributed the FY2025 revenue decline in that segment to "the challenging freight market cycle" [FY25 10-K, MD&A p.57; segment-map §1]. Mobility flags discretionary-travel and large-metro/airport-trip concentration (15% of FY25 Mobility Gross Bookings) as a risk [segment-map §1]. | Mobility and Delivery showed real demand sensitivity in the one severe shock on record (COVID), and Freight is a smaller but currently-depressed cyclical segment sitting inside the same consolidated results. |
| Disclosure quality *(higher = better)* | 67 | Rich, consistent platform KPIs are disclosed quarterly and annually — Gross Bookings, Trips, MAPCs, Revenue Margin, and segment Adjusted EBITDA, all by segment [business-identity §3a; segment-map §1]. Segment definitions have been stable since FY2023 [segment-map §3]. Offsetting this: Uber changed its segment profitability measure from Segment Adjusted EBITDA to Segment Operating Income starting Q1 FY26, impairing FY25-vs-FY26 margin comparability [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Note 10], and does not disclose segment-level balance-sheet assets because "the CODM does not evaluate operating segments using asset information" [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.112]. | Strong operating-KPI disclosure by the standard of the sector, held back by a mid-stream metric change and no segment asset/ROIC visibility. |

## 2. Aggregate Quality Score

**Aggregate: 46/100 (Mixed / Average band).**

Row scores sorted low to high: Competitive intensity 28, Regulatory dependence 28, Rate-of-change 32, Customer stickiness 35, Cyclicality 47, Pricing power 50, Margin stability 50, Recurring revenue 55, Disclosure quality 67, Commodity dependence 78, Capital intensity 85. The second-lowest row score is 28 (regulatory dependence), which caps the aggregate at roughly 48 — 46 sits inside that band. The weighting is not a straight average: competitive intensity, regulatory dependence, and industry rate-of-change dominate the read because together they describe the structural forces most likely to compress Uber's economics or change who wins the ride-hailing/delivery category over the next few years — a low score on any one of these caps how much credit the very strong capital-intensity score (85) can add. Capital intensity and commodity dependence are treated as secondary, real strengths (low fixed-asset burden, no direct commodity exposure) that improve the operating-model quality but cannot offset a business facing well-capitalized competitors, live driver-classification litigation in multiple jurisdictions, and an unresolved autonomous-vehicle transition.

## 3. Strongest Factor & Weakest Factor

| | Factor | Score | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Strongest | Capital intensity | 85 | Capex is ~0.6% of FY2025 revenue ($308–336M vs. $52,017M) — Uber owns no vehicles or trucks; Drivers, couriers, and Carriers carry the fixed-asset burden [Financials_Annual.xls, Cash Flow tab; FY25 10-K, Note 13]. |
| Weakest | Competitive intensity (tied with Regulatory dependence at 28) | 28 | The company's own risk factors describe "well-established and low-cost alternatives... low barriers to entry, low switching costs, and well-capitalized competitors in nearly every major geographic region," naming Bolt, Didi, Lyft, Ola, DoorDash-class rivals, and Waymo/Zoox/Tesla in autonomous vehicles [FY25 10-K, p.2478, p.2502, p.2529]. |

## 4. Read

Uber is a capital-light, high-frequency two-sided marketplace that took roughly a decade to become durably profitable (consolidated EBITDA margin only turned positive in FY2022 and has since risen steadily to 12.1% in FY2025) but operates in a structurally crowded field with low switching costs on both the rider and Driver side, active driver-classification litigation across multiple countries, and an unresolved autonomous-vehicle transition where Waymo already runs a competing robotaxi fleet. This reads closer to a scaled, asset-light operating platform than a durable, hard-to-dislodge compounder — the moat, to the extent one exists, rests on network liquidity and habit rather than switching costs or regulatory protection. The industry rate-of-change / disruption-risk row scored 32 (≤40), so this thesis is closer to a sector / technology-cycle bet than a durable compounder (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 5): the eventual balance of power between platform aggregators (Uber) and vertically integrated AV operators (Waymo) is not yet knowable, and that uncertainty should cap conviction independent of Uber's current financial performance.

RF-BQ-005 (fast-changing industry: rate-of-change ≤40)

The single quality factor a buyer should watch over the next 24 months is regulatory dependence — specifically driver-classification outcomes in the US, EU, and other active jurisdictions (score 28, the joint-weakest factor). FY2025 EBITDA margin of 12.1% and Mobility segment Adjusted EBITDA margin of 26.6% are near-peak, post-recovery readings on a business that ran negative EBITDA margins for its first six disclosed years (FY2016–FY2021) [Financials_Annual.xls, Ratios tab]; the through-cycle level is meaningfully lower than the current print once the one severe demand shock on record (FY2020 revenue down 14.3%, COVID) and the still-cyclical Freight segment (FY2025 Adjusted EBITDA margin -0.6%, "challenging freight market cycle") are weighted in [FY25 10-K, MD&A p.57]. A moderate Cyclicality score of 47 should be read alongside these peak-adjacent margins, not separately from them — the moat and DCF layers should treat FY2025's margin level as a recent high-water mark still building a multi-year track record, not a stabilized steady state.

## business-model / 08_competitive-map.md

_Source: `business-model/08_competitive-map.md`_

# Competitive Map — UBER

## 1. Dominant Segment

Mobility (ride-hailing) is the dominant segment: 57.0% of FY2025 revenue ($29,670M of $52,017M) and 69.1% of FY2025 total segment Adjusted EBITDA ($7,899M of $11,438M) [upstream: `03_segment-map.md`, citing FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.112–114].

## 2. Named Competitors

Uber's own FY25 10-K names its Mobility competitors explicitly: "We also compete with other ridesharing companies for Drivers and Riders, including Bolt, Didi, Lyft, and Ola," plus autonomous-vehicle developers Alphabet (Waymo), Amazon (Zoox), and Tesla [FY25 10-K, Item 1, "Competitive Environment," p.5]. Of the four named ridesharing rivals, Lyft and DiDi Global are public with disclosed financials; Ola (ANI Technologies, India) is privately held with no financials in this data pool; Bolt (Bolt Technology OÜ, Estonia) is privately held but discloses annual results via press statements. The three most credible — a comparable-scale public peer, a global-scale public peer, and a named regional rival — are profiled below.

### Competitor A — Lyft, Inc.

- **Ticker / listing:** NasdaqGS: LYFT
- **Where they compete:** US and Canada ridesharing marketplace (peer-to-peer rides, Express Drive vehicle rental, bikes/scooters); no meaningful Delivery or Freight overlap [Capital IQ Comp export, Business Description sheet, as-of 2026-08-06].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue $6,516.6M (filing date 2026-05-08), roughly one-eighth of Uber's LTM total revenue of $55,227M over the same comp window [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Financial Data sheet, as-of 2026-08-06]. LTM revenue grew 9.36% year-over-year, versus 16.68% for Uber over the same comp window [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics sheet, as-of 2026-08-06].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM EBITDA margin -0.1% (EBITDA -$6.7M on $6,516.6M revenue) and LTM EBIT margin -2.2% (EBIT -$145M) [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Financial Data and Operating Statistics sheets, as-of 2026-08-06]. LTM net income margin is reported at 43.8% in the same export — this is inconsistent with a negative EBIT and is very likely a one-off item (e.g., a tax-related gain), which the export does not itemize; treat the net-margin figure as unreliable for operating comparison and not from filings-level detail. ROIC/ROE: not disclosed in this data pool.
- **Source named in:** FY25 10-K, Item 1, "Competitive Environment," p.5 (named directly); also Uber's own Capital IQ comparable-company set [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Business Description sheet].
- **One-line read:** The closest same-business, same-geography peer — a smaller, thinner-margin US/Canada rideshare pure-play that Uber outgrew on revenue over the trailing year (16.68% vs. 9.36%) [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics sheet, as-of 2026-08-06].

### Competitor B — DiDi Global Inc.

- **Ticker / listing:** OTCPK: DIDI.Y (delisted from NYSE in 2021; trades over-the-counter)
- **Where they compete:** Ride-hailing and related mobility services in China (China Mobility segment), plus an International segment covering Brazil, Mexico, and other markets — geographic overlap with Uber mainly in Latin America, not China [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Business Description sheet, as-of 2026-08-06]. Note: Uber itself holds a minority equity stake in Didi, taken when Uber sold its China ride-hailing business to Didi in 2016 — the two are simultaneously named competitors and Uber is a minority shareholder in Didi [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p. (line ref ~3095), "a significant portion of our assets includes minority ownership positions, including in Didi, Grab, and Aurora"].
- **Scale:** LTM total revenue $34,391.3M (filing date 2026-06-02) — larger than Uber's LTM total revenue of $55,227M is not the case; DiDi's LTM revenue is about 62% of Uber's consolidated LTM revenue, and roughly 116% of Uber's Mobility-segment-only FY25 revenue ($29,670M), reflecting DiDi's own China-scale ride volume [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Financial Data sheet, as-of 2026-08-06]. LTM revenue grew 10.04% year-over-year [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics sheet, as-of 2026-08-06].
- **Profitability / return on capital:** LTM EBITDA margin -1.6% (EBITDA -$564.3M), LTM EBIT margin -2.6% (EBIT -$910M), LTM net income margin -1.1% [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics sheet, as-of 2026-08-06]. ROIC/ROE: not disclosed in this data pool — DiDi has not reported a positive operating profit in this comp window, so a return-on-capital figure would be negative and is not separately broken out.
- **Source named in:** FY25 10-K, Item 1, "Competitive Environment," p.5 (named directly as a Mobility competitor); also disclosed as a minority-investment holding in FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors.
- **One-line read:** Global-scale by revenue but structurally unprofitable over the trailing year, and only a partial competitor to Uber in practice — the two compete in Latin America while Uber holds a minority stake in Didi's dominant China business rather than contesting it directly.

### Competitor C — Bolt Technology OÜ

- **Ticker / listing:** Private (Estonia) — no public listing, no SEC/exchange filings.
- **Where they compete:** Ridesharing and micromobility marketplace focused on Europe, Africa, and parts of Latin America — a regional rival rather than a global-scale one [FY25 10-K, Item 1, "Competitive Environment," p.5, named alongside Didi, Lyft, and Ola].
- **Scale:** Reported 2025 revenue of €2.27 billion (up 14% year-over-year), equivalent to roughly $2.6 billion at the 2026-08-08 EUR/USD spot rate of ~1.155 [Web: "Bolt hits €2.27 billion in revenue, posts first-ever annual profit," Trade with Estonia, 2026 (unverified, dated); FX rate: Federal Reserve H.10, 2026-08-06]. This is roughly one-eleventh of Uber's Mobility-segment-only FY25 revenue ($29,670M) — outside the ~5x comparable-scale guideline, but included as a named, clear regional rival per the selection criteria rather than for scale comparability.
- **Profitability / return on capital:** Reported 2025 operating profit of €19.5 million (operating margin ~0.9%), reversing an €87.7 million operating loss in 2024, and a net profit of €0.9 million — Bolt's first profitable full year since founding in 2013 [Web: "Bolt posts first-ever profit in 2025," Zag Daily, 2026 (unverified, dated)]. ROIC/ROE: not public / not disclosed — Bolt does not publish a balance sheet.
- **Source named in:** FY25 10-K, Item 1, "Competitive Environment," p.5 (named directly).
- **One-line read:** A much smaller, only-just-profitable regional challenger in markets (Europe, Africa) where Uber's own risk factors admit it does "not have a leading category position" in every geography.

## 3. Competitive Position

Position vs peers: **Holding to gaining in the US, not disclosed globally.** In the US — Uber's home market and the one segment with third-party share data in this pool — Uber holds an estimated 76% of the US rideshare market versus Lyft's 24% [Web: Bloomberg Second Measure, US rideshare data, 2026 (unverified, dated)]; Uber's own FY25 10-K discloses no numeric market-share figure, only a qualitative claim to "global leadership position" [FY25 10-K, Item 1, p.4] alongside an explicit admission that "in certain geographic markets and regions, we do not have a leading category position" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p. (line ref ~2577)]. As a growth proxy, Uber's LTM total revenue grew 16.68% versus 9.36% for Lyft and 10.04% for DiDi over the same trailing window [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics sheet, as-of 2026-08-06] — consistent with share stability-to-gains against its two named public peers, though the comparison blends currency and cross-segment effects and is not a clean like-for-like Mobility-only read. Outside the US, position is **not disclosed**: Uber does not compete head-to-head with Didi in China or with Grab in Southeast Asia (Uber exited both markets via 2016 and 2018 stock-swap deals and now holds minority equity stakes in each instead of operating there directly) [FY25 10-K, Item 1A Risk Factors, p. (line ref ~3095)], so no consolidated global share figure is meaningful.

## 4. Competitive Shape

Uber's own 10-K frames the market as globally fragmented with low barriers to entry: "We compete on a global basis in highly fragmented markets... in the future we expect to face competition from new market entrants given the low barriers to entry that characterize these industries" [FY25 10-K, Item 1, "Competitive Environment," p.5]. In practice the shape is better described as **regionally concentrated, globally fragmented**: the US is close to a duopoly (Uber ~76% / Lyft ~24%) [Web: Bloomberg Second Measure, 2026 (unverified, dated)]; China is dominated by Didi, where Uber holds a minority stake rather than competing directly; Southeast Asia is dominated by Grab, on the same minority-stake basis; and Europe/Africa/Latin America remain more fragmented, with Bolt as the largest independent regional challenger alongside Uber, Didi (in Brazil/Mexico), and local players (e.g., Ola in India, not profiled above for lack of public financials). A separate but adjacent signal of ongoing consolidation: Uber has agreed to acquire a majority stake in Delivery Hero SE — one of the companies its own 10-K names as a Delivery competitor — for an equity value of roughly €12.9 billion ($14.8 billion), expected to close in the second half of 2027, explicitly described in deal reporting as a move to "better compete with DoorDash Inc. outside the US" [Uber-Technologies-Inc-NYSE-UBER-Key-Developments.txt, M&A announcement 2026-07-16 / pre-deal reporting]. This is a Delivery-segment, not Mobility-segment, development, but it signals that Uber is actively consolidating named competitors rather than only competing against them.

## 5. Caveat

Ola (ANI Technologies), the fourth Mobility competitor named directly in Uber's FY25 10-K, is privately held with no financial disclosures in this data pool; it could not be profiled with sourced scale or profitability figures and is therefore omitted from the three-competitor list above rather than profiled with invented numbers. The Bolt and Bloomberg Second Measure figures used in Sections 2–4 are dated web sources (Tier 10 in the source hierarchy) rather than filings or Capital IQ exports, and are labelled accordingly — they should be treated as directional, not audited. DiDi's segment-level China vs. International revenue split (needed to isolate the actual overlap with Uber in Latin America) is not broken out in the Capital IQ comp export available in this pool.

## business-model / 09_moat.md

_Source: `business-model/09_moat.md`_

# Moat — UBER

## 1. Named Competitors

(Inherited from `08_competitive-map.md`, itself sourced to Uber's own FY25 10-K, Item 1, "Competitive Environment," p.5.)

- **Lyft, Inc.** (NasdaqGS: LYFT) — closest same-business, same-geography peer: US/Canada ridesharing only, roughly one-eighth of Uber's LTM revenue, thinner margins.
- **DiDi Global Inc.** (OTCPK: DIDI.Y) — global-scale by revenue (~62% of Uber's LTM revenue) but structurally loss-making; overlaps with Uber mainly in Latin America, not China, where Uber instead holds a minority equity stake in DiDi itself.
- **Bolt Technology OÜ** (private, Estonia) — regional challenger in Europe/Africa, ~1/11th of Uber's Mobility revenue, only just turned its first annual profit in 2025.
- Ola (ANI Technologies) is also named directly in the 10-K but omitted from scoring here — private, no financials in the data pool [`08_competitive-map.md` §5].

## 2. Moat Sources

| Possible Moat | Present? (Y/N) | Evidence | Strength /100 |
|---|---|---|---:|
| Brand | Y (weak) | Uber holds an estimated 76% US rideshare share vs. Lyft's 24% [Web: Bloomberg Second Measure, US rideshare data, 2026 (unverified, dated), cited via `08_competitive-map.md` §3], suggesting real awareness/preference. But the company's own filing undercuts brand-driven pricing power: "consumers have a propensity to shift to the lowest-cost or highest-quality provider" and Uber "has in the past lowered, and may continue to lower, fares or service fees" to compete [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, competition risk factors, cited in `06_value-chain.md` §3]. A brand strong enough to defend share but not strong enough to defend price is a weak moat source. | 35 |
| Cost advantage | Y | Mobility segment Adjusted EBITDA margin rose from 22.4% (FY24) to 26.6% (FY25) [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.114, cited in `07_business-quality.md` §1] — a real, growing cost efficiency versus Lyft's roughly break-even LTM EBITDA margin (-0.1%) on one-eighth the scale [`08_competitive-map.md` §2, Competitor A]. The advantage looks like scale economics (fixed platform/tech and insurance costs spread over ~8x more volume) rather than a structurally lower unit cost that a well-funded rival cannot replicate — Lyft and DiDi run the same driver-payment and insurance cost structure, just at smaller scale. | 55 |
| Distribution | Y | 15,000+ cities in 70+ countries, 202 million MAPCs (Q4 FY25), and 13,567 million trips (FY2025) [FY25 10-K, p.1, p.49, cited in `02_business-identity.md` §1] give Uber a distribution footprint no named competitor matches outside China/Southeast Asia (where Uber does not operate directly). Uber One (46 million members) cross-sells Mobility, Delivery, and grocery off the same distribution base [FY25 10-K, p.1]. | 60 |
| Scale | Y | Uber's LTM total revenue ($55,227M) is roughly 8x Lyft's ($6,516.6M) and about 1.6x DiDi's ($34,391.3M) [`08_competitive-map.md` §2, Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, as-of 2026-08-06]. Scale alone is not proof of a moat (DiDi is larger than Lyft and still loss-making), but combined with the cost-advantage row above it is a real, evidenced gap against Lyft specifically. | 60 |
| Technology / IP | N | The 10-K frames autonomous-vehicle technology as a competitive THREAT, not an owned advantage: Uber "may fail to offer autonomous vehicle technologies on our platform at competitive scale, fail to offer such technologies... before our competitors" and Waymo "has already launched its own commercialized robotaxi fleet independent of Uber's platform" [FY25 10-K, p.2229, p.2744, cited in `07_business-quality.md` §1]. No patent portfolio or proprietary-technology claim is cited anywhere in the pool as a barrier to Lyft, DiDi, or Bolt, all of whom run comparable matching/routing/dispatch apps. | 15 |
| Licenses / regulation | N | Regulation reads as a shared cost burden across all named competitors, not a differentiator that favors Uber over them — the 10-K describes ridesharing being "blocked, capped, or suspended" in multiple countries and active driver-classification litigation across many jurisdictions [`10_external-dependency.md` §1, "Regulation" and "Government policy" rows, both rated High dependence]. Lyft, DiDi, and Bolt already hold operating licenses in their respective markets; this is not a barrier that keeps them out. | 15 |
| Network effects | Y | Uber's own filing names the mechanism directly: it must maintain "critical mass" of Drivers and Riders in each city or "supply liquidity" degrades [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, "critical mass" risk factor, cited in `06_value-chain.md` §1]. More drivers online shortens wait times, which attracts more riders, which attracts more drivers — a textbook two-sided network effect, and Uber's larger scale (row above) means this loop runs faster for Uber than for Lyft in shared markets. The effect is real but bounded: riders and drivers "commonly multi-home across Uber, Lyft, Bolt, Didi, Ola with no lock-in mechanism beyond habit" [FY25 10-K, p.1763, p.2502, cited in `07_business-quality.md` §1] — multi-homing lets supply and demand split across platforms instead of tipping to one winner. | 50 |
| Switching costs | N | The 10-K states this as a risk factor in its own words: "the low switching costs between competitor platforms or services" threatens Driver and consumer retention [FY25 10-K, p.2666, cited in `07_business-quality.md` §1]. No contracts bind riders, eaters, or drivers to Uber [`07_business-quality.md` §1, Repeat/recurring revenue row]. This is a company admission, not an inference. | 10 |
| Natural resource access | N | Not applicable — Uber owns no vehicles, fuel supply, or extractable resource; Drivers and Carriers own and fuel their own vehicles [`07_business-quality.md` §1, Capital intensity row]. | 0 |
| Location advantage | Y (narrow) | Airport curbside access is a real, scarce point of leverage: 15% of FY2025 Mobility Gross Bookings originated at airports, where "airport authorities can restrict or ban ridesharing... or fail to renew operating agreements" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, "geographic concentration" risk factor, cited in `06_value-chain.md` §2]. Holding an existing airport operating agreement is a real advantage over a would-be new entrant, but the filing frames it as a risk Uber must defend, not a proven exclusivity versus the three named competitors (Lyft also holds airport agreements in its US/Canada markets). | 25 |

No single source above clears a "strong" bar (≥61) on its own. The closest to a real, durable edge — network effects reinforced by scale and cost advantage — is capped by explicit, filing-disclosed multi-homing and low switching costs on both sides of the marketplace.

## 3. Competitive Economics

| Company / Competitor | Gross Margin | EBIT Margin | Return on capital (ROIC, or ROE for financials) | Period | Source |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| Uber Technologies (UBER) | 40.8% | 12.1% | 14.7% (own calc, normalized tax, avg. capital, net-of-cash) / 9.4–10.6% (CIQ vendor figure, FY25/LTM) | LTM (as-of 2026-08-06); ROIC base year FY2025 (Dec-31-2025) | Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics sheet, as-of 2026-08-06; Financials_Annual export, Ratios & Income Statement & Balance Sheet tabs, CIQ; FY25 10-K, Note 13 |
| Competitor A — Lyft, Inc. | 35.6% | -2.2% | Not disclosed | LTM (filing date 2026-05-08) | Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics sheet, as-of 2026-08-06, per `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |
| Competitor B — DiDi Global Inc. | 15.6% | -2.6% | Not disclosed (would be negative — no positive operating profit in this comp window) | LTM (filing date 2026-06-02) | Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export, Operating Statistics sheet, as-of 2026-08-06, per `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |
| Competitor C — Bolt Technology OÜ | Not disclosed | ~0.9% (operating margin, self-reported) | Not disclosed (Bolt does not publish a balance sheet) | FY2025 | Web: "Bolt posts first-ever profit in 2025," Zag Daily, 2026 (unverified, dated), per `08_competitive-map.md` §2 |

**The economic moat test.**

> Return on capital **mixed — at-to-modestly-above cost of capital on the latest year/LTM read, but below it on a 5-year through-cycle average**: FY2025 ROIC (own calc, normalized 21% tax rate, average invested capital net-of-cash) **14.7%** vs estimated WACC **~9.7%** (+~500bps); CIQ vendor "Return on Capital" **9.4%** (FY2025) / **10.6%** (LTM) vs the same ~9.7% WACC (roughly flat to +90bps); but the CIQ vendor series' own 5-year through-cycle average (FY2021–FY2025: -9.4%, -4.9%, +3.1%, +6.0%, +9.4%) is **+0.85%**, roughly **-885bps below** the same ~9.7% WACC — [Capital IQ Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab, "Return on Capital %" row, CIQ; WACC = CAPM estimate, Inference not from filings, basis below].

- **Metric match:** Uber is an operating company (asset-light two-sided marketplace, not a bank/insurer/REIT) — ROIC vs WACC is the correct pairing, consistent with `07_business-quality.md` §0's sector-overlay finding of "no match" (generic operating-company grammar applies).
- **Cross-check of the headline figure.** I computed my own NOPAT ÷ average invested capital rather than accept the CIQ vendor's "Return on Capital %" row at face value: **NOPAT (FY2025) = Operating Income $5,565M × (1 − 21% normalized tax rate) = $4,396M** [FY25 10-K, Note 13, p.114 (Operating Income); tax-rate basis below]. **Invested capital, net-of-cash** = Total Debt (LT debt + current portion + finance/operating leases, $12,302M FY2025-end) + Total Equity ($28,083M) − Cash & ST Investments ($7,633M) = **$32,752M** (FY2025-end) / **$29,843.5M** (FY2024–FY2025 average) [Financials_Annual export, Balance Sheet tab, CIQ]. That gives **ROIC = $4,396M ÷ $29,843.5M average = 14.7%** — materially higher than the CIQ vendor's own 9.4% (FY2025) / 10.6% (LTM) "Return on Capital %" figure on the same Ratios tab. **This is a real divergence and is flagged, not smoothed over**: the CIQ figure's exact denominator/tax treatment is not disclosed in the export, so it cannot be fully reconciled from this pool; possible explanations include CIQ including the ~$9.4B of non-operating long-term equity-stake investments (Aurora, DiDi, Grab — whose gains/losses already sit below Operating Income and are excluded from my NOPAT) inside its capital base, which would dilute the return, or CIQ using the actual (unnormalized) reported tax rate in some years of its average. Per the conservative default (CLAUDE.md §4), **the lower, vendor-sourced figure is used as the primary read for the verdict below**, while my own computed figure is shown for transparency.
- **Gross-capital check (cash-netting sensitivity).** Uber is close to net-debt-neutral rather than deeply net cash (CIQ "Net Debt/EBITDA" = 0.011x for FY2025, essentially zero) [Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab, CIQ], but cash-netting still matters: on a **gross-capital basis (no cash netting)** — Invested Capital = Total Debt + Total Equity, average $37,148.5M (FY2024–FY2025) — the same $4,396M NOPAT gives **ROIC = 11.8%**, about 290bps lower than the net-of-cash figure (14.7%). Shown alongside per the required net-cash sensitivity check; the effect here is real but moderate, not the dramatic collapse a true net-cash balance sheet would produce.
- **Normalized tax rate, stated and stripped.** The ROIC numerator uses a **normalized 21% structural tax rate** (the US federal statutory rate stated in Uber's own tax-rate reconciliation table) [FY25 10-K, Income Taxes note, "Federal statutory income tax rate... 21.0%"], **not** the distorted GAAP reported rates. FY2024's reported effective tax rate was **-139.6%** and FY2025's was **-74.9%** (both tax BENEFITS, not expenses) [FY25 10-K, Income Taxes note, p. (Effective tax rate table)] — driven entirely by two one-off, non-cash items: a **$6.4 billion release of US federal and state deferred-tax-asset valuation allowances in Q4 2024**, and a **$5.0 billion release of the Netherlands deferred-tax-asset valuation allowance during FY2025** [FY25 10-K, Income Taxes note, "2025 Compared to 2024"]. Using either reported rate in NOPAT would overstate the operating return by tens of percentage points on a one-off, non-recurring accounting event. Analyst consensus estimates a forward effective tax rate of roughly 18–21% for FY2026 and beyond [UberTechnologies EstimatesReport, Consensus tab, Effective Tax Rate % row, CIQ], corroborating 21% as a reasonable structural anchor. **This 21% rate is the anchor for `valuation/04_intrinsic-dcf` to reconcile to, since this module runs first.**
- **Through-cycle basis, latest year labelled peak.** `07_business-quality.md` §4 explicitly labels FY2025's margins as "near-peak, post-recovery readings on a business that ran negative EBITDA margins for its first six disclosed years (FY2016–FY2021)," and flags Freight as still cyclically depressed (FY2025 segment Adjusted EBITDA margin -0.6%, "challenging freight market cycle"). Consistent with that read, the CIQ "Return on Capital %" series was negative every year from FY2017 through FY2022 and only turned positive in FY2023 (+3.1%), rising to FY2024 (+6.0%) and FY2025 (+9.4%) [Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab, CIQ]. **Uber has not yet run a positive-return-on-capital year through a demand shock** — its one severe downturn on record (COVID, FY2020 revenue -14.3%) landed while the company was still deeply negative on this metric. The 3-year post-turnaround trend (FY2023→FY2025: 3.1%→6.0%→9.4%) is genuinely improving but is not a "through the cycle" track record in the sense of having been tested by a downturn while already profitable.
- **Cost-of-capital basis.** No company-disclosed WACC or hurdle rate exists in this pool (the 10-K's own "weighted-average cost of capital analysis" language appears only in a purchase-accounting/goodwill-impairment estimation-methodology footnote, with no rate given [FY25 10-K, Note 1 / Note 3 accounting-policy language]). **Estimated via CAPM, Inference, not from filings**: risk-free rate 4.6% [Web: 10-year US Treasury yield, ~4.6–4.65%, early August 2026 (dated, unverified)]; beta 1.15 (5-year) [Capital IQ Comparable Analysis export / Public Company Profile, as-of 2026-08-06]; equity risk premium 5.0% (standard long-run US estimate, not company-disclosed — Inference); cost of equity = 4.6% + 1.15 × 5.0% = **10.35%**. Cost of debt: pre-tax ≈ interest expense $440M ÷ LT+current debt $10,521M FY2025 = **4.2%**, after the same 21% normalized tax = **3.3%**. Weights from market values: equity $139,261.7M, total debt $14,731M (E/(D+E)=90.4%, D/(D+E)=9.6%) [Public Company Profile, CIQ, priced 2026-08-05]. **WACC = 0.904 × 10.35% + 0.096 × 3.3% ≈ 9.7%.**

## 4. Where The Company Sits

1. **Relative to peers:** Uber sits at the **top of named peers** on margin and capital efficiency. LTM gross margin (40.8%) and EBIT margin (12.1%) both beat Lyft (35.6% / -2.2%) and DiDi (15.6% / -2.6%); Uber is the only one of the three CIQ-covered names with a positive EBIT margin and a positive, disclosed return on capital [`08_competitive-map.md` §2; Section 3 table above]. Bolt is smaller and only marginally profitable (operating margin ~0.9%).
2. **Absolute (the economic moat test):** Uber's return on capital sits **at-to-modestly-above** its estimated cost of capital on the latest fiscal year and LTM read (CIQ 9.4%/10.6% vs ~9.7% WACC; own-calc 14.7% vs ~9.7% WACC), but **below** its cost of capital on a 5-year through-cycle average (+0.85% vs ~9.7% WACC) — the decisive test, since a single peak-adjacent year should not carry a moat verdict on its own (§3 above).

## 5. Moat Verdict

**Narrow moat.** The strongest evidenced source is the combination of **network effects + scale + cost advantage**: Uber's own filing names "critical mass" of Drivers and Riders as something it must actively maintain, its scale (~8x Lyft's revenue) supports a Mobility Adjusted EBITDA margin (26.6%, FY2025) far above any named public peer, and this margin gap now finally translates into a positive, peer-leading return on capital. But two things cap it at Narrow rather than Strong. First, the filing itself discloses the two features that most directly blunt a network-effect moat — low switching costs and common multi-homing across Uber, Lyft, Bolt, DiDi, and Ola — so the advantage defends share more than it defends price. Second, and decisively per the hard rule: Uber's return on capital has been above its estimated ~9.7% cost of capital only for the last 1–2 years (CIQ Return on Capital: +6.0% FY2024, +9.4% FY2025, +10.6% LTM), following a decade of value destruction including its one severe demand shock on record (COVID) landing while returns were still deeply negative; the 5-year through-cycle average (+0.85%) remains far below cost of capital. This is a moat that has only just crossed into being economic, not one proven sustained through a cycle — the durability test over the next five years is whether Uber can hold a return on capital above ~9.7% through the next demand downturn and through the unresolved autonomous-vehicle transition, where Waymo already operates a competing fleet independent of Uber's platform [`07_business-quality.md` §1, rate-of-change row, scored 32/100 — a fast-changing-industry flag per CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 5, that discounts durability further].

**Moat trajectory: Widening.** Evidence over the last five years is one-directional and specific: CIQ Return on Capital rose from -4.9% (FY2022) to +3.1% (FY2023) to +6.0% (FY2024) to +9.4% (FY2025) to +10.6% (LTM); EBIT margin rose from -5.7% (FY2022) to +2.98% (FY2023) to +6.4% (FY2024) to +10.7% (FY2025) to +12.1% (LTM); Mobility segment Adjusted EBITDA margin rose from 22.4% to 26.6% (FY2024→FY2025) [Financials_Annual export, Ratios tab, CIQ; FY25 10-K, Note 13]. Uber also grew LTM revenue faster (16.68%) than Lyft (9.36%) or DiDi (10.04%) over the same trailing window [`08_competitive-map.md` §2–3], consistent with share stability-to-gains rather than erosion. The widening trend is real but should be read alongside the low rate-of-change/disruption score (32/100) in `07_business-quality.md` — an AV-driven change in industry structure could interrupt this trajectory faster than the multi-year trend line alone would suggest, so the widening read should not be extrapolated mechanically into `valuation/04_intrinsic-dcf`'s durable-advantage period without discounting for that risk.

# External Dependency Check — UBER

## 1. Dependency Table

**Note on direction:** the risk score in Section 4 is inverted — higher number means MORE dangerous external dependence, not better.

| External Variable | Dependency Level (Low / Mid / High) | Why It Matters | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Commodity prices (fuel/gas, vehicle parts) | Mid | Uber does not own the vehicle fleet, so fuel and vehicle costs sit with Drivers and Carriers, not on Uber's own income statement. But when those costs rise, Drivers "spend less time providing services on our platform or seek alternative sources of income," which thins the driver supply Uber's network depends on. | "Factors such as inflation, increased fuel prices, and increased vehicle purchase, rental, insurance, or maintenance costs...have and may continue to increase the costs incurred by Drivers and Carriers...A decreased supply of Drivers...would decrease our network liquidity" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.~65 area, "Legal and Regulatory / Operational Risks" section] |
| Interest rates | Low | Uber's credit agreement (revolver) is undrawn, so a rate move does not hit interest expense there. The only quantified effect is a fair-value swing on existing fixed-rate notes, a balance-sheet mark, not a cash cost. | "Our primary exposure to market risks for changes in interest rates relate primarily to our credit agreement of which we currently have no drawn amounts as of December 31, 2025...A hypothetical 100 basis point increase in interest rates would have decreased the fair value of our notes by $538 million as of December 31, 2025" [FY25 10-K, Item 7A, p.67] |
| FX | Mid | Revenue outside the US and Canada was $25.55 billion of $52.02 billion total FY2025 revenue (49.1%) — [US&CAN $26,469m; LatAm $3,327m; EMEA $16,364m; APAC $5,857m; Total $52,017m — FY25 10-K, Note 13, Geographic Information]. Almost half of revenue converts back to US dollars every quarter. Uber hedges transaction/remeasurement exposure with forward contracts but says this "does not entirely eliminate" the effect, and it does not hedge translation of overseas revenue growth itself. | "We are exposed to foreign currency risks related to our revenue and operating expenses denominated in currencies other than the U.S. dollar...changes in exchange rates may negatively affect our future revenue and other operating results as expressed in U.S. dollars" [FY25 10-K, Item 7A, p.67]. Full-year FY2025 Gross Bookings grew 19% as reported vs. 20% on a constant-currency basis — a roughly 1-point FX drag for the year [FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.~55]. |
| Freight / logistics rates | Mid | Uber Freight (the third segment) sells directly into the trucking/freight brokerage market. Freight revenue was $5.10 billion of $52.02 billion total FY2025 revenue (~9.8%) and it is the one segment where Uber's own results moved backward with the external cycle. | "Freight Gross Bookings declined 1% year-over-year, on a constant currency basis, as a result of challenging freight market cycles" [FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.~55]; Mobility $29,670m, Delivery $17,248m, Freight $5,099m of $52,017m total FY2025 revenue [FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.~50]. |
| Government policy | High | Government tax and labor policy has already moved Uber's reported revenue by roughly $1.1 billion in a single quarter. Effective January 2, 2026, a UK legislative change forced Uber UK to stop applying the VAT Order 1987 and restructure how Mobility revenue is recognized, cutting Q2 FY26 revenue by $1.1 billion (and $2.1 billion for the first half of 2026) versus what it would otherwise have reported. Separately, HMRC has assessed Uber roughly $1.8 billion (£1.4 billion) in disputed back-VAT for 2022–2024, which Uber paid under protest to keep appealing. Mexico's Congress passed a 2024 law reclassifying higher-earning mobility/delivery workers as employees with profit-sharing rights. | "Effective January 2, 2026, we implemented a business model change in certain UK markets, primarily driven by regulatory and tax considerations...payments to drivers are recorded as a reduction of revenue instead of cost of revenue" and "negatively impacted revenue by $1.1 billion" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, filed Aug-05-2026, MD&A, p.~34]; "multiple assessments from...HMRC disputing our application of VAT Order 1987...totaling approximately $1.8 billion (£1.4 billion)" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Note 11, Commitments and Contingencies]; "in December 2024, the Mexican Congress passed a bill to amend Mexico's Federal Labor Law and reclassify all mobility and delivery earners who make more than one minimum salary a month as employees" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.12]. |
| Regulation (labor classification, licensing, data/privacy, antitrust) | High | The single largest disclosed risk factor is that Drivers could be reclassified from independent contractors to employees. Uber states this "would require us to fundamentally change our business model" and force "significant price increases for Riders." The company is fighting this in courts and legislatures in the US (California AB5/Prop 22), France (French Supreme Court cases through 2025), Switzerland, Spain, the Netherlands, and New Zealand (a November 2025 Supreme Court ruling found four drivers were employees while logged in). Airport and metro-level licensing is also concentrated risk: 15% of 2025 Mobility Gross Bookings came from airport trips, an activity many airports separately license or ban. | "If, as a result of legislation or judicial decisions, we are required to classify Drivers as employees...we would incur significant additional expenses...any such reclassification would require us to fundamentally change our business model" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, "Our business would be adversely affected if Drivers were classified as employees...", p.11-12]; "in November 2025, the New Zealand Supreme Court ruled that four drivers are employees while logged into the Uber app" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.12]; "In 2025, we generated 15% of our Mobility Gross Bookings from trips that either started or were completed at an airport" [Q2 FY26 10-Q, Item 1A, p.~48]. |
| Weather | Low | Weather is named only as one of several factors ("economic, social, weather, and regulatory conditions") that could hit the large-metro areas Uber concentrates in. It is not separately quantified or singled out anywhere in the filings — it rides alongside bigger, better-evidenced risks rather than standing on its own. | "As a result of our geographic concentration, our business and financial results are susceptible to economic, social, weather, and regulatory conditions or other circumstances in each of these large metropolitan areas" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.~17]. |
| Geopolitics | Low | War and sanctions are named as a factor pushing up fuel and vehicle-part costs (an indirect, already-captured channel via commodity prices/consumer cycle), and as a general source of "regional instability." Uber does not disclose material direct revenue exposure to Russia or an active conflict zone (Uber exited Russia via a JV structure years before this filing period). | "the broader consequences of conflicts in the Middle East and the conflict between Russia and Ukraine, which may include additional international sanctions, embargoes, regional instability, and geopolitical shifts...cannot be predicted" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.~26]; fuel-price linkage: "increased fuel prices as result of the conflict between Russia and Ukraine and the conflict in the Middle East" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.~17]. |
| Consumer cycle | Mid | Both Mobility and Delivery ride on discretionary consumer spending. Uber names unemployment, consumer debt, falling net worth, and consumer confidence as direct drivers of Gross Bookings, and specifically flags Delivery (food spend) as more exposed than Mobility because it is more purely discretionary. Airport-trip concentration (15% of Mobility Gross Bookings) adds a travel-cycle sub-exposure. | "Our performance is subject to economic conditions and their impact on levels of discretionary consumer spending. Some of the factors...include general economic conditions, unemployment, consumer debt, reductions in net worth...and other macroeconomic factors" and "because spending for food purchases from merchants is generally considered discretionary, any decline in consumer spending may have a disproportionate effect on our Delivery offering" [FY25 10-K, Item 1A, p.~17]. |
| Industrial cycle | Mid | Freight is the direct read-through to industrial/trucking demand, and it is the one segment that shrank in FY2025 while the other two grew double digits — evidence the exposure is real, not theoretical. It is roughly a tenth of consolidated revenue, which limits (but does not remove) the read-through to total results. | "Freight Gross Bookings declined 1% year-over-year, on a constant currency basis, as a result of challenging freight market cycles" [FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.~55]; Freight = $5,099m of $52,017m FY2025 revenue (~9.8%) [FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.~50]. |

## 2. Sensitivity, If Disclosed

| Variable | Disclosed sensitivity | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Interest rates | A hypothetical 100 basis point (1.00 percentage point) increase in interest rates would reduce the fair value of Uber's outstanding fixed-rate notes by $538 million (a balance-sheet fair-value effect, not a cash-flow or earnings effect, since the revolver is undrawn) | FY25 10-K, Item 7A, p.67 |
| Interest rates (investments) | A hypothetical 100bp change in rates "would not have a material effect on our financial results and on the fair value of our marketable debt securities," given the short-term nature of the portfolio | FY25 10-K, Item 7A, p.67 |
| FX (implied, not a stated sensitivity coefficient) | FY2025 full-year Gross Bookings: +19% reported vs. +20% constant-currency (~1-point FX drag for the year). Q2 FY26 Gross Bookings: +24% cited in revenue discussion vs. +22% constant-currency for the "Overall" line (implying FX was a modest tailwind that quarter, working in the opposite direction of the FY2025 full-year drag) | FY25 10-K, MD&A, p.~55; Q2 FY26 10-Q, MD&A, p.~34 |
| UK VAT/business-model change (government policy, not FX) | Cut reported Mobility revenue by $1.1 billion in Q2 FY26 alone and $2.1 billion for H1 FY26, versus the prior operating model | Q2 FY26 10-Q, MD&A, p.~34 |

Uber does not publish a formal "X% move in currency = $Y revenue/EPS impact" sensitivity table (unlike commodity-heavy industrials); the FX read above is inferred from the reported-vs-constant-currency growth gap, which is Level 4–5 evidence (the filing's own reconciliation) but not a stated coefficient.

## 3. Classification

**Partly externally driven** — Uber has real, working management levers: it does not own vehicles (fuel/vehicle-cost risk sits with Drivers, not Uber), it hedges transaction-level FX with forward contracts, it can and does adjust fares, service fees, and Driver/Courier incentives to manage supply and demand, and it has repeatedly defended its independent-contractor model in court and at the ballot box (Prop 22 in California, the 2024 Massachusetts settlement, favorable 2025 French Supreme Court rulings). But the exposure is not cosmetic: government tax/labor policy has already cut a full quarter's revenue by roughly 8% in one country alone (the UK VAT change), a US-style employee reclassification remains explicitly disclosed as capable of forcing Uber to "fundamentally change" its business model, ~49% of revenue is non-US-dollar, and one full segment (Freight, ~10% of revenue) tracks an external industrial cycle Uber does not control. This is a company with strong internal levers sitting on top of a policy and regulatory environment that is actively, not hypothetically, moving results.

## 4. External Dependency Risk Score

**54/100** (inverted scale — higher = worse / more dangerous external dependence)

This sits in the "material external exposure, mixed mitigation" band. It is pulled up from the bottom of that band by government policy already having a demonstrated, quantified P&L effect (the UK VAT/business-model change) rather than being a purely hypothetical risk-factor line, and by the driver-classification risk being explicitly disclosed as capable of forcing a "fundamental" business-model change if it goes against Uber in a major market. It is kept out of the 61–80 "mostly externally driven" band because Uber's asset-light model, active FX hedging, segment mix skewed toward the two faster-growing and less-cyclical segments (Mobility + Delivery = ~90% of FY2025 revenue), and a real track record of winning or settling classification fights (Prop 22, Massachusetts, the 2025 French rulings) give management levers that a pure pass-through business would not have.

## 5. The Single Biggest Lever

Government/regulatory policy on Driver classification and revenue-recognition rules is the single biggest lever: the UK's January 2026 VAT/business-model change already cut one quarter's revenue by $1.1 billion (about 8% of that quarter's $14.2 billion) in a single mid-sized market, and the FY25 10-K discloses that a similar employee-reclassification ruling in a major market such as the United States "would require us to fundamentally change our business model" — a shock of that kind in Uber's largest market (US&CAN was 50.9% of FY2025 revenue) would do more damage than an equivalent 20% adverse move in FX, fuel costs, or the freight cycle.

# Capital Allocation & Governance — UBER

## 1. Signal Table

Severity is INVERTED — higher score = worse.

| Signal | Observation | Evidence | Severity /100 *(higher = worse)* |
|---|---|---|---:|

Announces Chief Financial Officer Changes, Effective February 16, 2026")]; [Board Members export — Ronald Sugar, Independent Chairman since Aug-2018; Dara Khosrowshahi, CEO since Sep-2017] | 25 |

## 2. Classification

**Capital allocation concerns.**

Day-to-day capital discipline has genuinely improved: buybacks now outrun stock-based-compensation dilution (share count down from a 2,091mm peak in Mar-2025 to 2,036mm by Mar-2026), leverage is modest (1.4x LTM Total Debt/EBITDA before the pending deal), the auditor is stable and unqualified, and cash conversion is strengthening. But this is overridden by a clear serial-acquirer pattern: Uber has done multiple material deals every year since 2019 (Careem, Postmates, Drizly — later shut down — Transplace, Foodpanda Taiwan, Trendyol GO, pending Getir), and on Jul-16-2026 signed the largest deal in its history — a $14.8bn equity-value takeover of Delivery Hero SE financed by a €14.2bn ($15.3bn) committed debt bridge that would roughly double gross indebtedness if drawn. Per this module's rejector-filter rule (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 4), a debt-funded deal of this scale relative to the company's own balance sheet caps this row's severity at ≥70 and the overall Capital Allocation Score at 50/100 regardless of how clean the buyback/leverage/auditor signals are on their own.

## 3. Most Material Signal

The acquisition pattern — specifically the pending Delivery Hero SE takeover — is the signal that would most change this classification if it deteriorates further. If the deal closes on the announced terms (equity value $14.8bn, financed via a €14.2bn debt bridge, expected close H2 2027), Uber's leverage would roughly double from the current 1.4x Total Debt/EBITDA, its multi-year record of shrinking net debt would reverse, and the newly-built buyback discipline (net share count falling since early 2025) would compete directly with debt service for cash. This single transaction is large enough, relative to Uber's own $140-190bn market capitalization and ~$12.4bn pre-deal debt stack, to overwhelm every other positive signal in this table — the buyback trend, the low leverage, and the stable auditor — if execution or integration disappoints, echoing the earlier Careem/Postmates/Drizly/Transplace cycle where at least one large deal (Drizly) was wound down within roughly three years of closing.

## 4. Capital Allocation Score /100

**50/100 — capped.**

**Rejector-filter cap applied (CLAUDE.md §24, Filter 4).** The acquisition-pattern row scored 80/100 severity — a clear serial-acquirer pattern culminating in a debt-funded deal (the pending Delivery Hero SE takeover, $14.8bn equity value funded by a €14.2bn committed bridge facility) that is large relative to Uber's own existing debt stack and a material fraction of its market value. Per MODULE_RULES.md, this trips Filter 4 and caps the Capital Allocation Score at 50/100 regardless of the cleaner signals elsewhere in the table (falling net share count, moderate pre-deal leverage, stable unqualified auditor, improving cash conversion). Absent this cap, the uncapped average of the other twelve rows (weighted toward the lower-severity signals — dividend policy, capex discipline, related-party transactions, auditor history, working capital) would imply a score in the high-60s to low-70s range; the cap overrides that reading and is the binding constraint here.

## business-model / 12_red-flags-sweep.md
